What you can do at this point: name a document anywhere, ask for it, and receive something that can point onward.

What's still broken: all three are specifications — paper. Somebody has to write the program.

sections.title: Node 13 — what the first browser actually was, as a program
sections.content:
The limitation: conventions on paper move no bytes.

In September 1990 Berners-Lee got a NeXT machine — a black magnesium cube, 25 MHz, 8 megabytes of memory, running a Unix-derived operating system of the kind Node 6 describes. Between October and December 1990 he wrote a program on it called WorldWideWeb, later renamed Nexus to stop it colliding with the name of the thing itself. On 20 December 1990 the first web page went up on info.cern.ch.

Here is that program, entirely, in terms of Part I. This is the definition of "browser" and it never changes; everything in the remaining twenty-six nodes is an elaboration of one of these four steps.

Step one — turn the URL into a connection. Take the string apart at the punctuation. Hand the host portion to DNS, which is itself a network request (Node 10) costing a round trip, and get back four bytes of IP address. Make a system call (Node 6) asking the kernel to open a TCP connection to that address on port 80. The kernel does the three-packet handshake, another round trip. It hands back a small integer — a file descriptor (Node 10).

Step two — write the request. Build the bytes GET /path\r\n — which, from Node 4, means putting the numbers 71, 69, 84, 32, 47… into a run of boxes. Make a system call: write these bytes to descriptor 7.

Step three — read the answer. Make a system call: read from descriptor 7 into this buffer, a region of boxes the program set aside. The kernel parks the thread (Node 7) — no CPU burnt, but this thread is doing nothing at all for the Node 8 round-trip time, tens or hundreds of milliseconds, hundreds of millions of instructions' worth. Bytes arrive; the kernel wakes the thread; it reads more, until the server closes the connection. Now the document exists as numbers in the program's own memory.

Step four — turn those bytes into pixels. Interpret the buffer as text under an agreed encoding (Node 4), find the angle brackets, work out the structure, decide where everything goes, and write red-green-blue values into the framebuffer region (Node 9) so the scanout hardware puts it on the glass.

A browser is a program that turns bytes from a socket into numbers in the framebuffer. [EXPLAIN]

That's it. That is the whole job description, in 1990 and today. A modern browser is thirty million lines of code because step four grew a rendering engine, a programming language, a security model and a compiler, and because step two grew defences against everything people tried to do with it — but the four steps are the same four steps.

Two things about that first program worth carrying forward

It was also an editor. WorldWideWeb didn't just display pages; you could edit them in place and save them back. Berners-Lee's model was that reading and writing the web were the same activity, and he has said for decades that losing this was the great mistake. It got lost for a boring reason: the browsers that followed were much easier to write if they only read, editing required a way to write back to a server that HTTP/0.9 didn't have, and by the time the protocol could, browsing had become a read-only habit. The web spent twenty years re-growing writing as forms submitted to programs (Node 17) — which is a far more complicated thing than editing a document, and is the entire reason web applications exist as a category.

It only ran on NeXT machines, of which almost none existed. So in 1991 Nicola Pellow wrote the line-mode browser, which worked on any terminal — no graphics, no mouse, links shown as numbers you typed. Ugly, and the reason the web could spread at all, because almost everyone's access to a computer in 1991 was a text terminal.

And then the decision that did more than any other: on 30 April 1993, CERN put the software into the public domain. Anyone could implement it, use it, sell it, with no fee and no permission. Two months later Minnesota announced Gopher licensing fees. That contrast is a large part of why you are reading this in a browser.

What you can do at this point: fetch a document from any machine on earth and get it into your own memory as bytes.

What's still broken: step four was one sentence pretending to be simple. "Work out the structure" is doing enormous work. You have a run of forty thousand boxes holding numbers that mean ASCII characters, some of which are angle brackets. That is not a document — it is flat, and the thing it describes is nested. Nothing so far can turn one into the other.

Next: Node 14 — from a run of bytes to a tree in memory, where the parser gets built as a state machine, the DOM turns out to be blocks of boxes holding each other's addresses, and browsers make the second great "accept broken input" trade of this series.

sections.title: Node 14 — from a run of bytes to a tree in memory
sections.content:
The limitation: the document arrived as a flat run of boxes holding numbers that mean characters. Flat is wrong. What the characters describe is nested.

A paragraph sits inside a section. A bold word sits inside the paragraph. A cell sits inside a row inside a table. The bytes are in address order, one after another, with no structure at all — structure is only implied by the angle brackets, and implication is not something a program can act on.

So the first real job is: build, in your own memory, a structure with the same shape as the thing the bytes describe.

Why a tree, and what a tree is in boxes

The shape is a tree because containment has exactly the properties of a tree: everything sits inside exactly one thing, and things nest without ever partially overlapping. You never have a paragraph that starts inside a table cell and ends outside it. (People write that, and Node 14's second half is entirely about what happens then.)

Now — what is a tree, in the row of numbered boxes from Node 2? There's no "tree" in memory any more than there's a letter. There are numbers. So you make a Node 4 agreement.

Take one element, say a paragraph. Set aside a block of consecutive boxes and agree that:

  • the first few boxes hold a number saying what kind of node this is (say 1 for element, 3 for text)
  • the next eight hold the address of the block for this node's parent
  • the next eight hold the address of the block for its first child
  • the next eight hold the address of the block for its next sibling
  • the next eight hold the address of a separate block listing its attributes
  • and for a text node, the address of a run of boxes holding the characters

That's a DOM node. A block of boxes whose fields are mostly the addresses of other blocks of boxes. [EXPLAIN] Eight boxes per address because modern machines use 64-bit addresses (Node 2), and 64 bits is 8 bytes.

Note what a "tree" then physically is: blocks scattered anywhere in memory, in no particular order, tied together only by the numbers they hold about each other. Draw it on paper and it's a neat tree; in memory it's confetti with addresses written on it.

Why hold addresses instead of just laying children out consecutively after their parent? Because the structure has to change. Insert a paragraph in the middle of a page laid out consecutively and you must shift millions of boxes along to make room. Insert it into the address-linked version and you write three numbers: the new block's next-sibling field, the previous sibling's next-sibling field, and the parent's first-child field if it went at the front. Three writes, a handful of instructions, regardless of document size. [EXPLAIN]

And now something you've written a thousand times is fully explained. document.body.firstChild.nextSibling reads the first-child address out of body's block, goes to that block, reads its next-sibling address, goes to that block. Three memory reads, a few hundred instructions in Node 8's terms — genuinely cheap. Whereas document.querySelectorAll('.item') must walk the entire confetti, following every address, checking every node's attributes. That's why one is free and the other isn't, and it isn't a rule about "the DOM being slow." It's what the two operations are made of.

One name to place: DOM stands for Document Object Model, and it is the agreed interface to this structure — the set of names and operations (firstChild, appendChild, parentNode) that a browser promises to offer. It was first standardised as DOM Level 1 in October 1998, after Netscape and Microsoft had each invented incompatible versions. The tree exists in memory whether or not anything ever asks about it; the DOM is the vocabulary for asking. In Node 18 that distinction becomes the whole story, because giving a program access to that vocabulary is what turns a document into an application. [EXPLAIN]

The parser, as a state machine

Now: how do you get from characters to blocks?

You read one character at a time and keep a variable saying what you're in the middle of. That variable is the state, and a program shaped like this is a state machine. [EXPLAIN] From Node 3 it's unremarkable — a number in a register, and a conditional jump that goes to different code depending on its value.

state = TEXT
for each character:
    if state is TEXT:
        if char is '<'  -> state = TAG_NAME, start collecting a name
        else            -> add char to the text being accumulated
    if state is TAG_NAME:
        if char is a space -> state = ATTR_NAME
        if char is '>'     -> the tag is complete; emit it
        else               -> add char to the name
    if state is ATTR_NAME:
        ...

Each complete tag or run of text that comes out is a token, and this half is the tokeniser. The real HTML tokeniser has around eighty states, because of quoted and unquoted attribute values, comments, doctypes, CDATA, script contents, and character references — but every one of them is this same shape.

Then a second stage turns the stream of tokens into the tree, and it needs to remember where it currently is in the nesting. It does that with a list it only ever adds to and removes from at one end — push an element when you see an opening tag, pop it when you see the matching closing tag. The element on the end is "the thing I'm currently inside," so any new node gets attached as its child.

Careful here, because two different things share a word. In Node 5, "the stack" meant a specific region of memory the CPU uses for function calls, with the stack pointer register. What we have now is a data structure used in the same disciplined way — add and remove at one end only — but it's an ordinary list in ordinary memory, built by the parser for its own bookkeeping. The word "stack" describes the discipline, not the location. The parser's stack of open elements and the CPU's call stack are unrelated things that happen to both be last-in-first-out. [EXPLAIN]

The decision that shaped the industry

What should the parser do when the document is wrong? And documents are wrong constantly — <b><i>hello</b></i>, a <p> never closed, an attribute value missing its closing quote, a </div> too many.

The clean engineering answer is: refuse. Report a parse error. That is what XML chose, and what XHTML tried to force onto the web around 2000, and it is why XHTML lost.

The answer browsers actually took, from the earliest ones and hardened for thirty years, is:

Never fail. Always produce a tree.

Because a parse error shown to a reader is useless. They didn't write the page, can't fix it, and don't care whose fault it is — they just see a broken browser and use a different one. A browser that renders the sloppy page beats a browser that is right about it, every single time. [EXPLAIN]

This is the same trade as Node 11's broken links, made again: give up correctness, win adoption.

And it has a very long tail. "Be lenient" is not a specification. So through the nineties every browser was lenient differently — one closed your unclosed <p> when it hit a <div>, another nested it — and identical bytes produced different trees in Netscape and Internet Explorer, which is the technical root of "works in one browser, broken in the other" and of a decade of writing every page twice.

The eventual fix, in the HTML5 work from roughly 2004 through 2012, was strange and correct: rather than defining what valid HTML means and leaving errors undefined, the specification defines exactly what to do for every possible malformed input — a big machine of "insertion modes" with precise rules for every unexpected token in every state. There's even a named procedure, the adoption agency algorithm, whose sole job is untangling misnested formatting tags like that <b><i>hello</b></i>. Thousands of lines of pure error recovery, written down so all browsers get the same wrong answer. [AWARE] The web's specifications largely stopped saying what pages should be and started saying what browsers must do.

Three more things the parser has to handle

It runs on bytes as they arrive, not on the whole document. From Node 10, the response comes in packets — 1500 bytes at a time, spread over Node 8's slow round trips. Waiting for the last one before starting would mean the screen stays blank until the whole thing lands. So the parser is incremental: it consumes whatever has arrived, builds what it can, and resumes when more comes. This is why you see a page appear progressively rather than all at once. [EXPLAIN]

It has to guess the encoding before it can read anything. Node 4: bytes are only characters by convention, and you must know which convention. But the declaration of the convention — <meta charset="utf-8"> — is itself inside the document, written in that convention. So browsers read the first chunk assuming something ASCII-compatible, hunt for a declaration in roughly the first kilobyte, and if they find a different one, throw away the tree so far and start again. If they find nothing, they guess from statistics and locale. That is the entire origin of pages full of â€™ — a guess that went the other way. [USE]

Some characters can't be written literally. < starts a tag, so a document that wants a literal less-than sign needs an escape hatch: <. Which makes & special too, so it needs &. These are character references, and the double-escaping bugs you've seen — &amp; displayed on a page — are exactly one round of this applied twice.

What you can do at this point: hold a document in memory as a structure a program can walk, from any input, however broken.

What's still broken: a tree of blocks holding each other's addresses is not something anyone can see. Not one pixel has been written.

sections.title: Node 15 — from a tree to pixels
sections.content:
The limitation: the tree describes structure; the screen from Node 9 is a grid of coloured dots. Nothing connects them.

Three passes, in order. Most of it is arithmetic.

Pass one: style — decide what each node should look like

Each node needs values: font family, size, colour, spacing, whether it stacks vertically or flows inline.

The first browsers hardcoded this — an <h1> was big and bold because the code said so. Every browser still has this as its floor: a built-in default stylesheet, which is why unstyled HTML isn't invisible, and why headings are bold and links are blue-and-underlined in a page with no CSS at all.

Authors wanted control immediately, and the first answer was to put appearance in the markup: <font color="red">, <center>, bgcolor. This works, and it is a disaster, because appearance is now welded to structure — restyling a thousand pages means editing a thousand pages, and the same paragraph can't be styled differently in two contexts.

CSS breaks the weld. Proposed by Håkon Wium Lie on 10 October 1994 (with Bert Bos; a W3C Recommendation in December 1996), its idea is: rules live separately and select nodes by what they are or what class they carry.

p.intro { font-size: 18px; color: #333; }

The browser matches rules against nodes and computes, for every node, a final value for every property. Which needs two extra mechanisms, both of which trip people constantly and both of which are just conflict resolution:

The cascade. Several rules can match one node, and they can disagree. So there's an ordering: rules from the browser's default stylesheet lose to rules from the page, later rules beat earlier ones, and more specific selectors beat vaguer ones — p.intro beats p. Specificity is literally a count of the id, class and element parts of the selector, compared piecewise. That's the whole algorithm, and it's why an id selector cannot be overridden by ten class selectors: it's not a weight, it's a higher column. [USE]

Inheritance. Some properties, if unset, take the parent's computed value — colour and font do, because you want to set them once on the body; borders and margins don't, because a border on every descendant would be absurd. Which properties inherit is a fixed per-property fact in the spec, not a rule you can derive. [USE]

The output of this pass is, per node, a complete set of values with nothing left unspecified. [EXPLAIN]

Pass two: layout — decide where everything goes

Now the arithmetic. Every node gets four numbers: x, y, width, height — a rectangle. The coordinate system has (0,0) at the top-left, x increasing rightward, and y increasing downward, which is a convention inherited from Node 9's scanout hardware sweeping the screen top to bottom, not from mathematics.

The interesting part is that layout is two directions at once, and this explains most layout behaviour that feels arbitrary:

Width flows down. A block element's width is determined by its parent's width — the parent knows how much room it has and hands it to the child. So width can be computed on the way in, top to bottom.

Height flows up. A paragraph's height depends on how many lines its text takes, which depends on the words, the font, and the width it was given. So the child computes its own height and reports it back, and only then does the parent know its own height, and only then does the parent's parent know. Height is computed on the way out, bottom to top. [EXPLAIN]

That asymmetry is why width: 100% is easy and "make this child fill the remaining height" was hard for twenty years until flexbox and grid gave the parent a way to do a second pass.

Inside a block, text is laid out by line breaking: measure each word's width in the chosen font, add it to the current line, and when the line exceeds the available width, start a new one. Each line is one font-height tall. Count the lines, multiply, and you have the paragraph's height. Genuinely: measure, add, compare, wrap.

This whole pass has a name in engine source code — layout, or reflow — and its cost is roughly proportional to how many nodes must be touched. [EXPLAIN]

And now the property that becomes the central performance fact of the browser: layout is not local. Change one element's width and every following sibling may move, which changes the parent's height, which moves everything after the parent. One small change can invalidate the geometry of the entire page. That coupling is the seed of Node 37, and the reason "just move this one thing" can cost more than it looks.

Pass three: paint — write the numbers

Every node now has a rectangle, a colour, a font. So walk them and write bytes into the pixel buffer from Node 9.

Fill a rectangle: a loop writing four bytes per dot. Draw a character: fonts are stored as outlines — mathematical curves describing the shape of each glyph — which get rasterised, meaning the curves are evaluated to work out which dots they cover and how much, producing a small greyscale bitmap that is then blended into the buffer at the right position in the right colour. Rasterised glyphs are cached, because you draw the letter "e" thousands of times per page.

Order matters, because things overlap and later writes cover earlier ones. So painting follows a defined sequence — backgrounds, then borders, then text, then anything positioned or z-indexed, in a defined stacking order. When two elements overlap and the wrong one is on top, this pass is where the answer lives.

In practice modern engines add a step: rather than painting everything into one buffer, they paint into several layers which the GPU then combines. That's what makes it possible to move something on screen without repainting anything — Node 37's subject entirely.

Putting the whole path together

For the first view of a page: bytes arrive over the slow connection (Node 10) → parsed incrementally into a tree of address-linked blocks (Node 14) → style computed per node → layout assigns rectangles → paint writes numbers into a buffer → the scanout hardware puts it on the glass (Node 9), 60 times a second, every 16.67 milliseconds.

That's a complete browser: fetch, parse, style, layout, paint. It is 1993, and it works.

What you can do at this point: display any document from any machine on earth.

What's still broken: the page is a photograph. It was computed once, from bytes fetched once. Nothing in it can change. The only way to see anything different is to fetch a whole new document and destroy this one.

sections.title: Node 16 — the browser people actually used, and the tag that changed everything
sections.content:
The limitation: the software existed and almost nobody could run it.

WorldWideWeb ran only on NeXT machines, of which very few existed. The line-mode browser ran anywhere and was text-only. Meanwhile several people built graphical browsers — ViolaWWW, Erwise, MidasWWW — mostly for Unix workstations, mostly by one or two people.

Then, in February 1993, the National Center for Supercomputing Applications at the University of Illinois released Mosaic, written by Marc Andreessen and Eric Bina. Three things made it the one that mattered.

It ran on machines people had. Unix first, then Windows and Mac later in 1993. That was the whole game: in 1993 the graphical web existed only for people with an expensive workstation, and Mosaic put it on office PCs.

It installed easily, with no compilation and no Unix expertise.

And it put images in the page. On 25 February 1993, Andreessen proposed the <img> tag on the www-talk mailing list. Berners-Lee didn't like it — it named one specific medium instead of a general mechanism for including any kind of resource, and there was a competing proposal to do the general thing. The general thing was better designed. Andreessen shipped <img> anyway, and it was in the browser everyone was using, so it won.

That is the first appearance of a pattern that runs through the next twenty-five years, and it's worth naming since it explains most of the weirdness in the platform: on the web, shipping beats specifying. A feature that exists in a browser people use becomes real, and standards bodies follow along afterwards writing down what happened. Node 39 is where that becomes an explicit policy.

Andreessen left NCSA, co-founded a company, and Netscape Navigator shipped in late 1994. Within a year it had the overwhelming majority of users. Microsoft, having nearly missed the internet entirely, licensed the Mosaic code from a company called Spyglass and shipped Internet Explorer 1.0 in August 1995, bundled with Windows — and the browser war began, which is Node 39's story.

For now, only the consequence matters: from 1994 onward, browser features were shipped as weapons in a commercial fight, fast, unilaterally, and incompatibly. Almost every strange corner of the platform dates from this period, including the entire subject of Part III.

What you can do at this point: millions of ordinary people can use the web.

What's still broken: they can only read. The web is a library, and everyone wants it to be a shop, a bank, a mail client.

sections.title: Node 17 — forms, CGI, and the wound
sections.content:
The limitation: the document is a photograph, and a photograph cannot take input.

The mechanism added was the form: <form> wrapping <input> fields and a submit button. Press submit, and the browser gathers every field's name and value, encodes them as name=value&name=value with special characters percent-escaped, and sends them to the URL in the form's action.

Two ways to send them, and the distinction is exactly this:

  • GET glues the encoded pairs onto the URL after a ?. So the whole request is a URL — bookmarkable, shareable, and re-sent identically if you reload. Which is right for a search and wrong for a payment.
  • POST puts them in a request body — bytes sent after the request headers. Not in the URL, not bookmarkable, and the browser warns before re-sending on reload. Right for anything that changes something. [USE]

(A request body needs a place to put it, which HTTP/0.9 from Node 12 didn't have. Forms are one of the reasons HTTP grew headers and a body — the version that has them, HTTP/1.0, was written down in 1996.)

On the other end, the server has to do something with those values, which means running a program rather than reading a file. CGI — the Common Gateway Interface, from the NCSA server in 1993 — defined the dumbest possible arrangement that works: when a request arrives for a certain path, start a program (a whole new process, Node 6), hand it the submitted values, and send whatever it prints back as the response. [AWARE] That's the origin of server-side programming as a job, and of every framework that followed.

And now the wound, which is the reason for everything in Parts III and IV

Look at the shape of the cycle this creates. Every interaction is:

  1. Discard the entire page — the tree from Node 14, all of it, gone.
  2. Open a connection and ask the server for a whole new page. Node 10: DNS, handshake, request, response. Node 8: a hundred-odd milliseconds at best.
  3. Wait.
  4. Parse the new document from scratch. Style it from scratch. Lay it out from scratch. Paint it from scratch.

Every one. Tick a checkbox that should reveal one extra field — full cycle. Get one field wrong in a twelve-field form — full cycle, and the page that comes back has often lost what you typed, because the server must re-render every value from its own memory and frequently didn't bother. Sort a table by a different column — full cycle.

And in 1995 the connection was a modem: 28.8 kilobits per second, about 3.6 kilobytes a second. A modest 40-kilobyte page is eleven seconds. The screen goes blank, then white, then redraws, and the thing you were reading is gone.

Put Node 8's numbers on it. During each of those waits, the chip in front of the user — running at three billion instructions a second — executes essentially nothing. It has the document tree sitting in its own memory, it has the framebuffer, it has all the capability built through ten nodes of Part I, and it is idle, because the document is a photograph and the only permitted action is to request a different photograph from a machine on another continent.

That is the wound. And note precisely what's wrong: it isn't that the network is slow. It's that the user's own machine is not allowed to do anything at all, so every change of any size must pay the full network cost.

What you can do at this point: build a real interactive application, as long as the user waits for a round trip on every single interaction.

What's still broken: there is no program running inside the page. Nothing on the user's machine can look at the tree, decide anything, or change one word on the screen without asking a distant machine for permission.

Part II is complete. Next: Part III — a program inside the page. Node 18 is ten days in May 1995, and the two design decisions made in that fortnight that dictate everything you have ever fought with in JavaScript.

sections.title: PART III — A PROGRAM INSIDE THE PAGE
Node 18 — ten days in May 1995
sections.content:
The limitation: the user's machine holds the document tree in its own memory and is not allowed to touch it, so every change of any size costs a full round trip to another continent.

The fix, stated from Node 17's wound, is forced: ship a small program along with the document, run it on the user's machine, and let it modify the tree from Node 14 in place. Change the tree, redo style and layout and paint (Node 15), and the screen changes with no network involved at all.

Simple to say. Four things have to be built for it, and each one is a decision that is still shaping your day.

First: what does "run a program" even mean here?

Node 3 says the CPU reads instructions out of memory — specific numbers meaning specific operations for that specific chip family. So one obvious way to put a program in a page would be to ship those numbers: the actual machine instructions.

Which fails immediately, twice.

It isn't portable. The numbers that mean "add these registers" on an Intel chip mean something else, or nothing, on the chips in a Mac of 1995 or a phone of today. A web page has to run on machines whose instruction sets hadn't been invented yet.

It isn't safe. Node 6 gave programs a private memory world and a kernel doorway, but within your world, machine instructions can do anything your process can do — read every box in your process, make any system call you're permitted, open your files. Downloading raw instructions from a stranger's website and running them is exactly the thing every security mechanism in Part I exists to prevent.

So you ship the program as text — Node 4, characters as agreed numbers — and the browser includes a program that reads that text and does what it says without ever handing it to the chip. That reading-and-doing program is an interpreter. [EXPLAIN]

How does an interpreter work? It's Node 14 again, applied to source code instead of markup. Read the characters, tokenise them into words and symbols with a state machine, build a tree in memory — for code this is called an abstract syntax tree, and an if statement becomes a block of boxes holding the address of its condition, the address of its "then" branch, and the address of its "else" branch, exactly like a DOM node holds the addresses of its children. Then walk that tree: to run an if, evaluate the condition subtree, look at the answer, walk one branch or the other. [EXPLAIN]

The crucial property is that the interpreter decides what is allowed. There is no instruction the script can express that the interpreter doesn't choose to carry out, because the script's "instructions" are just nodes in a tree the interpreter is walking. The page's code never becomes the chip's code. Want to forbid reading arbitrary memory? Don't offer an operation that does it. That's the entire foundation of browser security, and Node 33 builds on it.

The price is speed. Walking a tree to do a + b costs hundreds of instructions where the chip would use one. Original 1995 JavaScript was roughly a hundred times slower than compiled code — completely fine for showing and hiding a menu, and the reason nobody in 1995 imagined writing an application in it. Node 38 is the story of that assumption being demolished.

Second: how does the program get into the page?

A new tag: <script>. When the parser from Node 14 encounters it, it stops emitting document nodes and hands the text inside to the interpreter.

And there is a detail here that has consequences for the rest of the web's history: **when the parser hits a <script>, it stops.** Parsing halts, the script runs to completion, and only then does parsing resume. If the script is in an external file, the parser stops and waits for the network — Node 8, hundreds of milliseconds, while the page is a blank screen.

Why would anyone design that? Because early scripts used document.write(), which injects text into the parser's own input stream at the point the script sits. The parser cannot continue past a script until the script has finished, because the script might change what comes next. It's not carelessness; it's a consequence of a feature nobody uses any more and everybody still pays for. Hence <script defer> and <script async>, and the folk rule about putting scripts at the bottom of the body — all of them workarounds for a 1995 decision about document.write. [USE]

Third: what can the program actually do?

By itself, nothing that matters. The language can add numbers and loop. What makes it useful is that the browser hands the interpreter a set of pre-made objects that reach into the browser's own memory: document, whose properties and methods read and modify the tree of blocks-holding-addresses from Node 14.

This is the whole point, and it's worth being blunt about it: JavaScript the language is not the interesting part. The interesting part is that a browser exposes its live document tree to an interpreter. Change a node's text through document, and you've written into the boxes the render pipeline reads from — so style, layout and paint (Node 15) run again and the screen changes. No connection, no handshake, no round trip. Node 17's wound, closed.

The names for that exposed vocabulary are the DOM from Node 14 — and in 1995 there was no standard for it. Netscape invented one set of names, Microsoft invented another (document.layers versus document.all), and for years every page was written twice with a test to decide which browser it was in.

Fourth: the program itself

Netscape hired Brendan Eich on 3 April 1995. The company had already decided to put a scripting language in the browser, and had a deal in motion with Sun to bundle Java — a serious, statically typed, compiled language, intended for "real" applications delivered as applets. Internal politics settled on: Java for programmers, and something small and forgiving for page authors and designers, who were not programmers and were not going to become them.

Eich wrote the prototype — Mocha — in ten days in May 1995. It shipped in the Netscape 2.0 beta in September 1995 as LiveScript, and was renamed JavaScript on 4 December 1995 as part of the Sun marketing arrangement. It has essentially nothing to do with Java: different design, different type system, different everything. The name was a business decision and it has confused people for thirty years. [AWARE] (When it was later standardised, in June 1997, "Java" was Sun's trademark, so the standard had to be called ECMAScript — after ECMA, the standards body. That's why the language has two names, one of which nobody uses in conversation.)

The ten days are visible in the language, and it helps to know which parts are accidents so you stop hunting for logic in them:

  • typeof null returns "object". In the original implementation, a value was tagged with a small number saying what it was, tag 0 meant "object", and null was represented as the all-zeroes pointer of Node 4 — so it read as tag 0. A bug, unfixable now because fixing it would break pages.
  • == converts types before comparing, with a table of rules nobody can recite, which is why === exists and why every style guide says use it.
  • Semicolons are inserted automatically when a line looks finished, which is usually right and occasionally silently wrong.

But two decisions from that fortnight are not accidents, and they run the entire rest of this series.

Decision one: it is event-driven

The script does not run, finish, and exit like a normal program. It mostly registers itself to be called later: "when this button is clicked, run this function."

So the program is a set of reactions with gaps of nothing in between. This isn't a style preference — it's the only shape that fits a program whose purpose is to react to a human who might click in three seconds or three minutes or never. A program that ran top to bottom and exited would have nothing to say about what happens afterwards.

Which means, mechanically, that the browser must hold onto the address of your function (Node 5: a function is a run of instructions at an address) and call it at some later moment. Everything in Part IV is about the consequences of handing your function's address to somebody else.

Decision two: exactly one thread ever touches the document

Node 7 built threads, and built the danger: threads in one process share memory, the timer interrupt can land between any two instructions, and a structure of blocks-holding-each-other's-addresses being modified by one thread while another walks it produces reads of half-detached nodes and freed memory — silently, intermittently, unreproducibly. The defence is locks, which are a specialist skill that produces deadlocks and once-a-week bugs.

The document tree from Node 14 is precisely such a structure. So Netscape's choice was: one thread, ever, touches the DOM and runs JavaScript. No locks, because there is no second toucher. No race conditions, ever. count = count + 1 cannot lose an increment in JavaScript, and that's a guarantee no multithreaded language can give you. [EXPLAIN]

The bargain is exact, and if you hold this sentence, most of Parts III and IV become predictable rather than memorised:

You get total immunity from concurrency bugs, and in exchange you may never, ever block.

Because with one thread, "blocked" doesn't mean "this function is waiting." Node 7: the instruction pointer is stuck inside your function, so it is not inside the click handler, not inside layout, not inside paint. The page is frozen.

What you can do at this point: change the page without touching the network.

What's still broken: "register to be called later" was asserted, not built. Who holds those addresses? What is running while your code isn't? There must be a program around your program, and nothing so far has described it.

sections.title: Node 19 — the loop that is always running
sections.content:
The limitation: event-driven code implies something that dispatches events, and that thing has no name yet.

Here it is, and it's smaller than its reputation.

The browser sets aside a region of memory holding a queue — a list where entries are added at one end and taken from the other, so the oldest is served first. Each entry is a small record: the address of a function to call, plus the arguments to call it with. And the browser runs this:

forever:
    if the queue is empty, ask the kernel to park this thread
    take the oldest entry out of the queue
    call that function, and wait for it to return
    if enough time has passed, run style, layout and paint

That's the event loop. [EXPLAIN] It is not a metaphor. It is a while loop over a list, written in the browser's own code (C++), and it is the outermost thing running on that thread.

Which means a sentence worth sitting with: your JavaScript is never "the program." Your JavaScript is a pile of functions that this loop occasionally calls. The program is the browser. You are a plugin.

Where the entries come from

Not from your thread. From everything else, using Node 7's machinery.

You press a key. The keyboard raises an interrupt (Node 6); the kernel handles it and delivers it to the browser process; browser code — running on a different thread, often in a different process — takes a lock on the queue, appends "call the keydown handlers with this key," releases the lock, and wakes the parked main thread if it's asleep.

An image finishes downloading. The bytes arrived over the network (Node 10) into a thread that was parked in a kernel wait list (Node 7). That thread appends "call the load handler" to the queue.

A timer expires. Node 20's subject, same mechanism.

And now the answer to a question that should be bothering you: if another thread has my data, why doesn't it just call my function? Because calling your function means running JavaScript, which means touching the DOM tree, which is exactly the shared structure Node 18 forbade a second thread from touching. So the only safe thing it can do is append to a list and walk away. The main thread calls your function itself, when it's ready. [EXPLAIN]

The line that governs everything: "and wait for it to return"

Wait for it to return. The loop cannot take the next entry until the current one finishes, because it is one thread with one instruction pointer (Node 3 and Node 7), and one instruction pointer cannot be in two places.

This has a name — run to completion — and it's a guarantee, not a limitation, from one angle: no other JavaScript can interleave with yours. Nothing preempts you. A hundred events can arrive while your function runs and all hundred wait in the queue. That's why you never need a lock.

From the other angle it's the whole problem. Write this:

const start = Date.now();
while (Date.now() - start < 5000) {}

and the instruction pointer spends five seconds inside that loop. Meanwhile the queue fills with clicks and keystrokes and timer callbacks, and not one of them runs. Style, layout and paint don't run, because the loop only reaches that line after your function returns. The tab is a photograph again — an unresponsive one, where the button doesn't depress and the cursor doesn't blink and the browser eventually offers to kill the page. [EXPLAIN]

Put Node 9's number on it. The screen wants a fresh buffer every 16.67 milliseconds. A piece of JavaScript that takes 500 ms means thirty frames that never happened — not "the browser got slow," but thirty scheduled repaints that could not occur because the loop was still inside your function. That's what jank is, physically.

This is cooperative multitasking, on purpose

Node 6 described the failure mode of Windows 3.1 and the classic Mac OS: no timer interrupt forcing a switch, every program expected to voluntarily yield, and one program that didn't froze the entire machine including the mouse.

That is exactly the model JavaScript uses, deliberately, for Node 18's reason. The main thread is not preempted. It yields only by returning. A tab that freezes is the 1993 Mac failure mode, alive and well, chosen on purpose because the alternative was handing locks to web authors.

Which reframes the whole platform. Every asynchronous API in the browser — and there are hundreds, and their asynchrony is the thing that has been exhausting you — exists because of this. Anything slow cannot be a function that computes and returns, because that function would hold the loop and freeze the page. So every slow thing is expressed the same way: start it, return immediately, and have something appended to the queue when it's done. Network, disk, decoding an image, asking permission for the camera: all of them, without exception. [EXPLAIN]

The asynchrony isn't fashion, and it isn't JavaScript being weird. It is one thread, one instruction pointer, and a promise not to freeze.

Where rendering fits

Notice the last line of the loop: if enough time has passed, run style, layout and paint. Rendering is not something that happens whenever the DOM changes. It happens between tasks, when the loop gets control back, and at most about sixty times a second because there's no point producing frames the screen won't scan out (Node 9).

Two things follow immediately:

Changing the DOM ten times in one function paints once, not ten times. The changes all land in the tree; the loop reaches the render step once, afterwards. So a loop that appends a thousand nodes doesn't cause a thousand reflows — it causes one, at the end. (Unless you read a geometric property like offsetHeight in between, which forces the browser to compute layout right now, mid-function, to give you a truthful answer. Do that inside a loop and you get the famous "layout thrashing": alternate write, forced read, write, forced read, and layout runs a thousand times.) [USE]

Nothing you do to the DOM is visible until you return. Set a "Loading…" message and then run a five-second computation, and the message never appears — the loop never reached the render step. This single fact accounts for an enormous share of "why doesn't my spinner show" confusion, and it isn't a bug anywhere; it's the loop's shape.

One historical note: none of this was specified for the first fifteen years. It was just what browsers happened to do, and they differed in the details. It was only written down properly in the HTML specification around 2010 onward, once the differences started breaking real applications. Node 39 again — the specification recording what already existed.

What you can do at this point: explain exactly why a page freezes, predict which code freezes it, and say why every browser API that touches something slow has the shape it has.

What's still broken: the queue only fills when something external happens. Your own code has no way to say "do this later" — so any long computation must run as one unbroken block, and there's no way to do anything on a schedule.

sections.title: Node 20 — timers, and the lie in setTimeout(fn, 0)
sections.content:
The limitation: only the outside world can put work in the queue. Your code cannot schedule itself.

setTimeout(fn, 1000) arrived with the language in Netscape 2.0, and it does exactly what Node 19's machinery implies. It writes down two things in a table the browser keeps — the address of your function (Node 5) and a target time — and returns immediately, within microseconds. Your function has not run. It has been written down. Later, when the event loop comes round and has nothing else in hand, it checks that table, finds entries whose time has passed, and appends them to the queue. Then, eventually, the loop takes them off and calls them. [EXPLAIN]

Which makes the delay you pass a minimum, not a promise. Ask for 1000 ms, and if at the 1000 ms mark the loop happens to be 400 ms into someone else's function, yours runs at 1400. Nothing is broken; there was one thread and it was busy (Node 19). Every "my animation drifts" and "my timer is inaccurate" question ends here, and no amount of API redesign can fix it without preemption, which Node 18 gave up on purpose.

setInterval(fn, 1000) is the same table with a repeat flag, and it has a specific trap worth naming: it schedules by wall clock, not by "when the last run finished." If your callback takes 1200 ms and the interval is 1000, the runs stack up back to back with no gaps and the page degrades in a way that looks mysterious. The standard fix is to not use it — call setTimeout again at the end of each run, so the gap is always measured from actual completion. [USE]

And now the one everybody meets and nobody is told the truth about.

**setTimeout(fn, 0) does not run fn now.** It appends it to the queue, which means it runs after the current function returns and after everything already queued. So it means, precisely:

"Yield. Let the loop breathe — process pending events, do a render pass — and then continue."

That is the only yielding primitive JavaScript had for its first twenty years, and it was how you broke Node 19's five-second freeze into something survivable: process a thousand items, setTimeout(rest, 0), return. The loop then dispatches queued clicks and runs style/layout/paint, and afterwards calls your next chunk. The page stays alive. [EXPLAIN]

It also isn't really zero. The HTML specification says that once you have five levels of nested timeouts, the minimum clamps to 4 milliseconds. That's a historical compromise: browsers found pages busy-spinning through zero-delay timers, burning laptop batteries, so a floor was added, and 4 ms was roughly where the harm stopped without breaking existing sites. There's no theory in the number, and knowing that saves you looking for one. [AWARE] (Browsers also throttle timers hard in background tabs — often to once a second — for the same battery reason, which is why a countdown in a hidden tab drifts.)

Three siblings exist, each aimed at a different part of the loop, and it's worth seeing them as one family:

  • **queueMicrotask(fn)** — jump ahead of everything in the ordinary queue. That's a second queue, and it's Node 27's entire subject.
  • **requestAnimationFrame(fn)** — run immediately before the next paint, so your change and the paint land in the same frame. Node 37.
  • **requestIdleCallback(fn)** — run only if the loop has spare time left in this frame. Node 37 as well.

What you can do at this point: schedule your own work, slice long work so the page stays responsive, and predict when a callback will actually run.

What's still broken: every bit of this only rearranges work the machine already has. Node 17's wound is completely untouched — to get new data, the page must still be thrown away and refetched.

Next: Node 21, where a feature built for Microsoft's webmail client in 1999 quietly ends the era of the page reload — and where the pleasant, obvious, synchronous API turns out to be physically impossible on one thread, which is the real answer to why all this async exists. Then Node 22 counts what callbacks cost, and Part IV begins.

sections.title: Node 21 — asking the server a question without throwing the page away
sections.content:
The limitation: new data still requires a full navigation, which destroys the document tree, the running script, and everything held in memory.

This is the hinge of the whole series, and the way it actually happened is stranger than the tidy version people tell.

It did not come from the web standards world. It came from Microsoft, and it came out of an email client.

The Exchange team was building webmail — Outlook Web Access — and hit Node 17's wall head-on. An email client where clicking a message in the list repaints the entire window, blanks the screen, and loses your scroll position is not an email client. It's a slideshow of an email client. So they built a thing JavaScript could use to make an HTTP request on its own and hand the response back to script, without navigating. It shipped in Internet Explorer 5, in March 1999, as an ActiveX component called XMLHTTP.

Mozilla reimplemented it natively in 2002 under the name XMLHttpRequest; Safari followed in 2004, Opera in 2005, and IE finally made it a native object rather than an ActiveX control in IE7 in 2006. [USE]

The name is a small monument to how accidental this platform is. The XML is there because XML was the fashionable data format in 1999 and was the intended payload — almost nobody has sent XML through it in twenty years. And the capitalisation is inconsistent (XMLHttp, not XMLHTTP) because of a typo that became permanent, since fixing it would break existing pages. The object on which the entire modern web was built is named after a format it doesn't carry, in a capitalisation that was a mistake.

The flag, which is the whole story

The original object had a third argument, and everything in Part IV descends from it:

var xhr = new XMLHttpRequest();
xhr.open("GET", "/messages", false);   // false = synchronous
xhr.send();
console.log(xhr.responseText);         // the data is right here

Look at that code. You call it, and on the very next line you have your data. No callback, no promise, no await, no chain, no nesting. A variable holds the answer. That is the API everybody says they want, and it existed, and it was there first.

And it is a catastrophe, for a reason we built two nodes ago and can now state exactly.

send() cannot return until the bytes arrive. So the instruction pointer (Node 3) sits inside send() for the entire round trip. Underneath, the thread makes a system call and the kernel parks it in a wait list (Node 7) — it burns no CPU, but it is unavailable, and it is the only thread there is. So the event loop (Node 19) is not looping. It cannot take the next entry off the queue, because it is not at the line where it takes entries; it is buried inside your function, inside send(), inside the kernel.

For Node 8's hundred milliseconds if the server is close and healthy. For several seconds if it isn't. For thirty seconds if it has hung. During which: no clicks, no scrolling, no keystrokes, no cursor blink, no style, no layout, no paint. The tab is frozen solid, and the browser eventually offers to kill the page.

The sentence this whole series exists to deliver

I want to state this as plainly as I can, because it is the actual answer to "why does all this asynchronous shit exist":

The pleasant API is not discouraged. It is not bad practice. On one thread, it is physically impossible.

One instruction pointer cannot both wait for a machine in Virginia and repaint your scrollbar. Given the single thread that Node 18 chose — and it chose it to make race conditions and locks impossible for web authors, which was the right call — these two properties are mutually exclusive:

  1. "The result is available on the next line."
  2. "The page keeps responding while we wait."

You may have either. Never both. The web picked the second, permanently, and **every awkward thing you have ever fought — callbacks, .then chains, async functions, functions that are "coloured", the fact that you cannot call an async thing from a normal one and just get the value — is the invoice for that choice.** It is not incidental complexity. It is the price, and it was paid deliberately, in exchange for a page that never freezes and a language with no locks.

Synchronous XHR is now formally deprecated and browsers log warnings when you use it. That's the standards world admitting the flag should never have existed.

So the flag became true

var xhr = new XMLHttpRequest();
xhr.open("GET", "/messages", true);
xhr.onreadystatechange = function () {
  if (xhr.readyState === 4 && xhr.status === 200) {
    render(xhr.responseText);
  }
};
xhr.send();          // returns immediately — no data yet

Trace it through every layer we've built, because this is the moment all of Part I pays off:

  • send() hands a request description to the browser's networking code and returns in microseconds. Your function's stack frame (Node 5) pops. The event loop (Node 19) takes the next entry. Clicks work; the page paints.
  • The waiting happens on a different thread, usually in a different process (Node 7): DNS lookup, TCP handshake, request written, thread parked in a kernel wait list, costing nothing (Node 10, Node 8).
  • Bytes arrive. That thread cannot call your function — it would be a second thread touching the DOM, which Node 18 forbade. So it does the only safe thing: takes the lock on the main thread's queue, appends an entry, releases, and wakes the main thread if it's parked.
  • The event loop, whenever it next finishes what it's doing, takes that entry off and calls your function itself.

readyState counting 0 through 4 is just a number in the object's block of boxes being updated as the request progresses; 4 means finished. It's crude, and it's honest about what's happening.

What this actually changed

The technique had no name until 18 February 2005, when Jesse James Garrett published an essay coining AJAX — Asynchronous JavaScript and XML. By then Google had shipped the proof: Gmail in April 2004 and Google Maps in February 2005, where you dragged the map and new tiles simply appeared, with no reload, and it was genuinely startling to see.

But name a deeper consequence, because it's the one that created the job you're applying for:

The page stopped being a document and became a long-lived program with its own memory. Before this, all application state lived on the server, and the page was a fresh photograph of it. After this, the page persists across interactions, holds state in its own variables, and asks the server only for data. So the server stopped rendering pages and started answering questions — which is what an "API" is. Frontend and backend became separate jobs, and the data format became JSON (Douglas Crockford, around 2001, standardised 2006), which won over XML because it maps directly onto the objects the language already had. [EXPLAIN]

And one more thing quietly became true, which Node 33 will spend itself on: a page can now silently make requests to any machine, in the background, without the user seeing anything. In 1995 a page could only fetch what it displayed. Now a script from any site can talk to any server, using whatever credentials the browser holds. Every browser security rule you have ever cursed at exists because of the sentence you just read.

What you can do at this point: build a real application in a single page — fetch data, update part of the screen, never navigate.

What's still broken: the only tool available is "hand your function's address to something and hope." That's fine for one request. Node 23 counts what it costs for three. But before that, there's a hole in Part I that's about to matter: a callback runs after the function that created it has returned, and it can still read that function's variables — which Node 5 said was impossible, because the frame is gone.

sections.title: Node 22 — where values actually live: the stack, the heap, and garbage collection
sections.content:
The limitation: Node 5 built the stack and was categorical about it — a function's locals live in its frame, and on return the stack pointer moves back and those boxes are available for the next call to trample. So this should be impossible:

function makeCounter() {
  let count = 0;                 // a local, in makeCounter's frame
  return function () {           // this function outlives makeCounter
    count = count + 1;
    return count;
  };
}
const next = makeCounter();      // makeCounter has RETURNED. Frame gone.
next();  // 1
next();  // 2   ... reading a variable in a frame that no longer exists?

makeCounter returned. Its frame was abandoned. And yet count is alive, remembers its value between calls, and is private to this one counter — make a second one and it has its own. Either Node 5 was wrong or something else is going on.

Something else is going on, and it's a whole region of memory I haven't shown you yet.

Two regions, two disciplines

Both are just parts of the row of numbered boxes from Node 2. What differs is how they're handed out.

The stack (Node 5): one moving boundary, allocation and release are a single register change, and everything is released in exactly reverse order. Ferociously fast — a call costs a few instructions. And rigid: a frame's lifetime is exactly the call's lifetime, no exceptions.

The heap: a large region managed by a bookkeeper program that tracks which chunks are in use and which are free. Ask for 64 bytes; it finds a free chunk, marks it used, hands back its address. Nothing about when it's released is tied to any function returning. A block can be created deep inside one call and still be there an hour later. [EXPLAIN]

The name "heap" is unhelpful — it isn't a pile and it has nothing to do with the heap data structure in algorithms. Read it as "the region where things live for as long as they need to, rather than until a function returns."

The heap costs more. Finding a free chunk of the right size takes real work, chunks get freed in a different order than they were taken so the space fragments into unusable gaps, and every allocation touches a bookkeeping structure. Tens to hundreds of instructions versus one. This is why languages that let you choose still care about the distinction. [EXPLAIN]

In JavaScript you don't choose. Every object, array, function and string lives on the heap. A variable holding an object holds the address of a heap block. Which explains, entirely, a thing that trips everyone:

const a = { n: 1 };
const b = a;        // copies the ADDRESS, not the block
b.n = 2;
console.log(a.n);   // 2 — same block, two variables holding its address

Nothing was copied except a number. That's also why === on two objects compares addresses, not contents, and why two structurally identical objects are never equal.

Who frees it?

In older languages, you. You call something to get a block and something else to give it back, and you get three failure modes: leaks (never give it back, memory grows until the process dies), dangling pointers (give it back and keep using the address, reading whatever occupies those boxes now — Node 4 says the boxes will happily contain something and won't tell you it's the wrong something), and double frees (give the same block back twice and corrupt the bookkeeper). These are a large fraction of all serious security vulnerabilities in software.

JavaScript takes that away from you, using an idea from John McCarthy in 1959, in Lisp: garbage collection.

Here's the actual mechanism, because it's simple and it explains every memory problem you'll ever have in a browser.

Start from the roots: the global object, and every variable in every stack frame currently live. Follow every address you find, and every address in every block you reach, marking each block as you go. When you can't reach anything new, every block you didn't mark is unreachable — no chain of addresses from any running code leads to it, so no code can ever refer to it again. Those blocks are free. That's mark and sweep. [EXPLAIN]

The critical word is reachable, not "used." The collector doesn't know what you want. It knows what you can still reach.

Which is the whole of memory leaks in JavaScript. A leak is never "forgot to free." It is always something is still reachable that you thought was finished: a listener still registered on a node you removed, a growing array of cached entries, a setInterval that was never cleared holding its callback, which holds its variables, which hold a large object. Reachable, therefore kept, forever. [USE]

Real collectors add a wrinkle worth knowing because it shows up in profilers: most objects die almost immediately (a temporary in a loop) while a few live forever (your app's main state). So V8 splits the heap into a small young generation, collected very often and very fast — usually under a millisecond, and made cheap by copying the few survivors out and declaring the whole region free — and an old generation for things that survived a few rounds, collected rarely and more expensively. And a collection is work on the main thread, which means it eats into Node 9's 16.67 ms frame budget; a large major collection is a real source of dropped frames, which is why modern V8 does much of it incrementally and on background threads. [AWARE]

And now the closure

With the heap in hand, the paradox dissolves.

When the interpreter compiles makeCounter, it can see that the inner function refers to count, which belongs to the outer function. So count is not put in the stack frame at all. It's allocated as a block on the heap — an environment record, holding the outer function's captured variables.

A function value in JavaScript is therefore not just a code address (Node 5). It's a heap block holding two things: the address of the code, and the address of the environment record. That pair is a closure. [EXPLAIN]

So when makeCounter returns, its stack frame is abandoned exactly as Node 5 said. Nothing is violated. But the environment block is on the heap, and the returned closure holds its address, and you hold the closure — so it's reachable, so the collector keeps it. count lives because someone can still reach it, and it dies when nobody can.

Two consequences fall straight out, without needing to be memorised:

**Each call to makeCounter allocates a fresh environment block**, so each counter is genuinely independent. Not a rule — a consequence.

A closure keeps its whole environment alive. Capture one number from a scope that also holds a 10-megabyte array, and if they share an environment record, the array is reachable through your closure and cannot be collected. That's the most common real memory leak in front-end code, and it's not mysterious once you can see the block.

Now look back at Node 21 and see what was actually being handed over:

xhr.onreadystatechange = function () { render(xhr.responseText); };

You did not hand over a code address. You handed over a closure — code plus a heap block holding xhr and anything else it referenced. The browser stored that address in its own memory, your function returned, its frame vanished, and thirty seconds later the loop called the closure and every captured variable was exactly where it was left, on the heap, kept alive by being reachable.

**Every callback in this series, every promise's stored reaction, and every suspended async function in Node 31 is this same object: a code address plus a heap block of captured state.** Which is why Node 31 will turn out not to need any new magic at all.

What you can do at this point: say where any value lives, why objects are shared rather than copied, what a leak actually is, and why a function can outlive the function that made it.

What's still broken: nothing about the shape of asynchronous code. You can hand over a closure, and that's still the only tool. Node 23 counts what that costs.

Next: Node 23 — the callback, and every single thing it costs — four specific damages, each of which will turn out to be a hole that the promise object in Node 24 is shaped to fill.

sections.title: PART IV — MAKING THE PENDING RESULT A VALUE
Node 23 — the callback, and every single thing it costs
sections.content:
The limitation: the only tool for "something slow finished" is to hand over a closure and hope.

From Node 22, we now know exactly what that hand-over is: a heap block holding a code address and an environment record of captured variables. The browser stores that address in its own memory; later the event loop calls it. Mechanically sound. Nothing mysterious left in it.

The problem is what happens when you need two of them in a row — which is most of real work, because the second question usually depends on the first answer:

getUser(id, function (user) {
  getOrders(user.id, function (orders) {
    getDetails(orders[0].id, function (details) {
      render(details);
    });
  });
});

People mock the shape — "callback hell," "the pyramid of doom" — and the indentation is the least of it. There are four real damages, and I want them named separately, because the promise object in Node 24 is shaped exactly like the negative space of these four.

Cost one: errors have nowhere to go

try/catch looks like it should work here. It doesn't, and the reason is pure Node 5.

Throwing an exception is a mechanical operation on the stack: the machine walks the pile of frames from the top downward, looking for a frame whose function has a handler registered for this region of its code. Finding one, it discards every frame above it — moves the stack pointer back past all of them — and jumps to the handler. An exception can only travel down the stack that currently exists. [EXPLAIN]

Now look at what the stack actually contains when your callback runs. It is not:

    getUser
    yourOuterFunction
    ...

Your outer function returned long ago; its frame was abandoned (Node 5). The stack when the callback runs is:

    yourCallback         ← the top
    the event loop       ← called it (Node 19)

That's the whole stack. Two frames. The try you wrote in the outer function isn't in a frame any more — that frame's boxes have been trampled by dozens of subsequent calls. So this:

try {
  getUser(id, function (user) { throw new Error("boom"); });
} catch (e) {
  // never runs. Not "usually not". Never.
}

catches nothing, ever. The throw walks down from yourCallback, finds no handler, reaches the event loop, and becomes an uncaught error reported to the console.

So the community invented a hand-rolled substitute, which Node.js then made a hard convention in 2009: error-first callbacks. Every callback takes (err, result), and every callback body starts with if (err) return handleIt(err). Manual error propagation, written by hand, at every level, forever — with the property that any level that forgets swallows the failure in silence, and nothing warns you. [EXPLAIN]

Cost two: you gave away control of your own function

You handed a heap address to somebody else's code. What are the guarantees?

There are none. Not "weak ones" — none, because nothing enforces any.

  • Will it be called? Maybe. If the library has a code path where it forgets, your program simply stops there, with no error and no crash. Real libraries had these paths.
  • Will it be called once? Or twice, on a retry? Callbacks called twice are a classic real bug, and if yours appends a row to a table, the user sees two rows.
  • Will it be called later, or immediately, synchronously, before the function you passed it to has even returned?

That last one is the nastiest, and it earned a name. In 2013 Isaac Schlueter — then running Node.js — wrote a post about it titled with the instruction "don't release Zalgo." The failure is this: a function that fetches from the network when it has to, but calls your callback immediately when the answer is cached. Now the order of execution changes depending on cache state:

let ready = false;
fetchThing(id, function (thing) {
  if (!ready) console.log("callback ran before setup finished");
  use(thing);
});
ready = true;

On a cache miss this is fine. On a cache hit, the callback runs during fetchThing, before ready = true executes. So the bug appears only on the second visit, only sometimes, and never in your tests. [EXPLAIN]

This is inversion of control: the decision about how and when your code runs has been moved out of your code and into a stranger's, and the language offers no way to state the terms.

Cost three: parallel work has to be hand-assembled, and everybody's version is subtly wrong

Three independent requests, act when all three are done. There is no construct for this. So you write it:

const results = [];
let done = 0;
function collect(i) {
  return function (err, data) {
    results[i] = data;
    done = done + 1;
    if (done === 3) render(results);
  };
}
getA(collect(0)); getB(collect(1)); getC(collect(2));

That works, and it's fifteen lines of bookkeeping for one idea, and it gets rewritten in every codebase, and the version above has a bug you may not have spotted: **if one request errors, done never reaches 3**, so nothing renders and nothing reports a failure. The page just sits there. Every hand-rolled version has one of these; they differ in which one.

And "act when the first one finishes" needs a different fifteen lines. And "these two in parallel, then that one" needs a different fifteen again. None of them can be written once in a library, because the pieces being coordinated aren't values — which is the next cost, and the deepest.

Cost four: a pending result is not a value

Take an ordinary synchronous function. Its result is a thing. You can put it in a variable, return it, store it in an array, pass it to code you didn't write, keep it for later, compare it. It exists, at an address (Node 22).

Now: what is the "result" of getUser(id, cb)?

It is not anything. There's no object, no address, nothing to hold. The outcome is an event that happens inside a function body at some future moment. You cannot return it, because by the time it exists your function has returned. You cannot put it in an array, because it isn't a value. You cannot hand it to a helper written by someone else, because there's nothing to hand.

This is why nothing composes. Composition means combining values with functions, and there is no value here. That's the actual, structural reason callbacks force everything to nest: the only place the result is reachable is inside the function body it was delivered to, so any work that depends on it has to be physically written inside that body, and any work depending on that has to be written inside the next one. The pyramid isn't a style failure. It's the shape the data forces. [EXPLAIN]

And there's a fifth thing, worth a sentence: there's no way to cancel. You handed over an address. There's no handle, nothing to call stop on, and no defined way to say "never mind." Navigate away mid-request and the callback fires anyway, into a page that no longer exists.

The realisation

Put the four costs side by side and the fix names itself:

The costWhat it needs
errors can't travelsomewhere for a failure to be recorded rather than thrown
no guarantees on your callbacksomething that enforces "once, and always later"
parallel is hand-rolledsomething that can go in an array and be handed to a helper
the result isn't a valuemake it a value

They are all the same fix. Make the pending result an object — a block of boxes on the heap, with an address.

Because the moment it has an address: it can be returned, so a chain can be flat instead of nested. It can hold a state field meaning "failed," so a failure can be recorded and passed along instead of thrown into a stack that isn't there. It can be put in an array and handed to a helper, so "wait for all of these" is written once by somebody competent instead of fifteen times by everybody. And the object itself can enforce the guarantees, because it controls when the stored reactions are run.

That object is a promise, and Node 24 builds it out of boxes.

What you can do at this point: name exactly what is wrong with callbacks, mechanically, in four independent ways.

What's still broken: all four.

sections.title: Node 24 — the promise, as a block of cells with a state byte
sections.content:
The limitation: a pending result has no representation, so it cannot be returned, stored, passed, or reasoned about.

Where the idea came from

Not from JavaScript, and not recently.

The concept appears in 1976, in a paper by Daniel Friedman and David Wise, and again in 1977 from Henry Baker and Carl Hewitt under the name future: a placeholder for a value that a computation hasn't produced yet. The word promise in this sense comes from Barbara Liskov and Liuba Shrira in 1988, in a paper about a distributed language called Argus, and their motivation is precisely Node 8's: calling a procedure on another machine takes forever, so return a placeholder immediately and let the caller carry on. In the 1990s Mark Miller's language E developed the idea further, including chaining operations onto a promise before it resolves.

So by the time JavaScript needed this, it was a thirty-year-old, well-understood idea. What JavaScript did was arrive at it the long way round.

2009 — the CommonJS group publishes Promises/A, a proposal sketching the interface. 2011 — jQuery 1.5 ships Deferred, which looked like a promise and behaved differently in ways that mattered (its then didn't chain or propagate errors properly), so code that mixed the two broke confusingly. 2012 — a group of implementers, tired of incompatible libraries, write Promises/A+: a small, brutally precise specification of exactly how then must behave, with a conformance test suite. Libraries like Q, when.js and Bluebird implement it and interoperate. 2015 — ECMAScript 2015 makes it part of the language (Chrome had shipped it in 2014).

That order matters: the standard was written down after the community had already converged, and it standardised the behaviour that had won. Same pattern as Node 16's <img> and Node 14's parser rules — the web's specs record, they rarely invent.

The object itself

A promise is a heap block (Node 22) holding four things:

  • a state field — one of three values: pending, fulfilled, rejected
  • a value field — the address of the result, once there is one
  • a reason field — the address of the error, if it failed (in practice one field serves both)
  • the address of a list of reactions — the closures to run when it settles

That's it. That is a promise. [EXPLAIN]

The state field is the load-bearing part, and one rule governs it:

It starts as pending, and it may change exactly once — to fulfilled or to rejected. After that it is frozen forever.

The word for "no longer pending" is settled. A settled promise's state and value can never change again. That single rule delivers three of Node 23's four costs, as we'll see in a moment.

Creating one

const p = new Promise(function (resolve, reject) {
  // this function runs IMMEDIATELY, synchronously, right now
  doSomethingSlow(function (err, data) {
    if (err) reject(err);
    else resolve(data);
  });
});

The function you pass in is called the executor, and it runs synchronously, during the new, before new Promise returns. That surprises people; it's just how it is. Its job is to start the slow thing.

resolve and reject are closures (Node 22) that the constructor created, each holding the address of this promise's block. Calling resolve(data) does exactly three steps:

  1. If the state field isn't pending, return and do nothing. (This is the "settle once" rule, enforced in three instructions.)
  2. Write fulfilled into the state field and the value's address into the value field.
  3. Walk the reaction list and schedule each one — put it on a queue, don't call it.

Note the shape of what just happened: a promise doesn't do any work. It doesn't start the network request, it doesn't know what the work is, it can't cancel it. It is a box that someone else fills in, plus a rule about the box. Almost every "the promise executes eagerly / lazily" confusion comes from expecting it to be more than a box.

Attaching a reaction

p.then(onFulfilled, onRejected);

then does one of two things depending on the state field:

  • Pending? Append a record — the two closures, plus a bit of bookkeeping — to the reaction list. Then return.
  • Already settled? Schedule the appropriate closure immediately.

And here is the property that kills Zalgo from Node 23: in both cases the closure is scheduled, never called inline. Even on an already-settled promise, then puts the reaction on a queue and returns; your callback runs after the current function has finished. So:

const p = Promise.resolve(42);   // already fulfilled
p.then(v => console.log("A", v));
console.log("B");
// always prints B, then A. Every time. On every machine. Forever.

There is no cache-hit-versus-cache-miss ordering difference, because the specification made it impossible to call a reaction synchronously. [EXPLAIN] (Which queue it goes on, and why it's a different queue from the one in Node 19, is the whole of Node 27.)

The four costs, checked off

"You gave away control." Now the object controls it. Settle-once is enforced by the state field, so your handler cannot run twice. Always-scheduled is enforced by then, so the ordering can't shift under you. You are no longer trusting a stranger's library to be careful; you are trusting a rule in an object that both of you use.

"The result isn't a value." It is now. p is a variable holding the address of a heap block. Return it from a function. Put it in an array. Hand it to code you didn't write. Store it. Attach a handler to it now, or in ten seconds, or twice from two unrelated modules — all of which work, because attaching is just appending to a list, and a settled promise handles a late attachment by scheduling immediately. Try any of that with a callback and there's nothing to hold.

"Parallel is hand-rolled." Once these are values in an array, Promise.all([a, b, c]) can be written once, correctly, by someone thinking hard about the error case — Node 28.

"Errors can't travel." Half-solved: a failure is now recorded in a field rather than thrown into a stack that doesn't exist. But recording it isn't the same as it reaching the right handler, and that needs then to return a new promise, which is Node 25.

One naming trap, since it bites everyone

Three words are used precisely in the specification and loosely in conversation:

  • fulfilled — settled with a value.
  • rejected — settled with a reason.
  • resolved — not a state. It means "this promise's fate has been tied to something." If you call resolve(x) where x is an ordinary value, it fulfils immediately.
