But if x is another promise, this promise is now resolved to that one — still pending, and it will adopt whatever the other one eventually does. That adoption is what makes chains work in Node 25, and it's why resolve and fulfill are not synonyms. [AWARE]

What you can do at this point: hold a pending result as a value, attach handlers to it whenever you like, and rely on it settling exactly once and never calling you synchronously.

What's still broken: then returns something, and we haven't said what. Until it returns a new promise, chains don't flatten and errors still can't travel from one step to a handler at the end. The pyramid is still a pyramid.

Next: **Node 25 — why .then() has to return a new promise**, where the pyramid flattens into a chain, and where the two-line rule that makes chaining work turns out to be the entire reason async/await is possible at all.

sections.title: Node 25 — why .then() has to return a new promise
sections.content:
The limitation: a promise holds one pending result. Real work is a sequence of them, each depending on the last, and nothing yet connects one to the next.

Node 24 left then doing a small job: append a reaction record to a list, or schedule it if already settled. And it left one question unanswered — **what does then give back?**

If the answer is "nothing," you've gained a value and lost nothing else, but the pyramid stays a pyramid:

getUser(id).then(function (user) {
  getOrders(user.id).then(function (orders) {
    getDetails(orders[0].id).then(function (details) {
      render(details);
    });
  });
});

Same nesting, more punctuation. The pending result is a value now, but you still can't use that fact, because there's nowhere to put it — the inner call happens inside the outer handler, so its promise is trapped there.

Unless then returns a promise of its own.

The rule

then creates and returns a new promise — call it p2 — that starts pending. The reaction record it appends to p1's list holds three addresses: your handler, p2, and the resolve/reject closures for p2 (Node 22 — closures over p2's block).

Then, when p1 settles and your handler eventually runs, **what your handler does decides what happens to p2**, by exactly three rules:

  1. Handler returns an ordinary value → p2 fulfils with that value.
  2. Handler throws → p2 rejects with what was thrown.
  3. Handler returns a promise → p2 does not fulfil with that promise. It adopts it: p2 stays pending, attaches its own resolve and reject to the returned promise, and settles later with whatever that one settles with.

Rule three is the whole game. [EXPLAIN]

That single rule is what flattens the pyramid, because it means "returning a promise from a handler" and "the next step continues from that promise's value" are the same thing:

getUser(id)
  .then(function (user)    { return getOrders(user.id); })
  .then(function (orders)  { return getDetails(orders[0].id); })
  .then(function (details) { render(details); });

Trace it as boxes. getUser(id) returns promise A, pending. .then(f1) creates promise B, pending, and appends a record to A's list. .then(f2) creates C, pending, appends to B's list. .then(f3) creates D, appends to C's list.

All of that happens immediately, synchronously, before any network response exists. Four promise objects on the heap, three reaction records, all pending. The entire chain is built up front; only the running is deferred. That's a genuinely useful thing to hold, because it explains why the chain's shape is fixed at the moment you write it and can't branch based on a value you don't have yet.

Then the network answers. A fulfils with user. Its reaction is scheduled; f1 runs and returns promise E from getOrders. Rule three: B doesn't fulfil with E, B adopts E. B stays pending, and B's resolve is attached to E. E settles with orders; B fulfils with orders; C's reaction is scheduled; f2 runs. And so on down.

Nesting became sequence, and nothing was added to the language to do it. It's one rule about what a returned value means.

The bug this makes obvious

Everyone writes this once:

getUser(id)
  .then(function (user) { getOrders(user.id); })   // no return
  .then(function (orders) { console.log(orders); }) // undefined

Without return, the handler returns undefined, which is an ordinary value, so rule one applies and p2 **fulfils immediately with undefined**. The next handler runs straight away with nothing, while getOrders' promise floats off with no one attached to it — so if it fails, that rejection has no handler either.

Before this node, that's a mysterious "my chain runs too early." After it, it's mechanical: you told the chain the step was finished. [USE]

Two details worth having

**Anything with a then method counts as a promise.** Rule three doesn't check that the returned object is a real Promise; it checks whether it has a callable then property, and if so treats it as one. Such an object is called a thenable. This is why jQuery's Deferred from Node 24's history could be mixed into native chains at all, and why any library's promise-like object interoperates without adapters. It's also why an object of yours that happens to have a then method will be mistaken for a promise and quietly awaited. [AWARE]

**Every .then allocates.** A new promise block plus a reaction record on the heap (Node 22), garbage-collected when the chain is done. A three-link chain is a handful of small allocations — irrelevant in almost every real case, and worth knowing exists rather than imagining then is free syntax.

What you can do at this point: write a dependent sequence of asynchronous steps as a flat chain.

What's still broken: if step two fails, what happens? A rejection has to get from wherever it happened to a handler somewhere, and nothing has said how it travels.

sections.title: Node 26 — errors that can travel
sections.content:
The limitation: Node 23 established that exceptions can only walk the stack that currently exists, and that when a reaction runs, the stack is two frames deep — your handler, and the event loop. Every try you wrote is long gone.

So a rejection needs a different road. And Node 25 just built one, without meaning to.

The pass-through rule

A reaction record holds two handlers: one for fulfilment, one for rejection. Either can be missing, because you usually only supply one.

When a promise settles, it looks at each record and asks which handler applies. And if that handler is missing, it does not stall and does not throw. It applies this rule:

**If there's no handler for how this promise settled, settle p2 the same way, with the same value.**

A rejection with no onRejected in the record simply **rejects p2 with the same reason**. Which then reaches the next record down the chain, and does the same again, and again, until it finds a record that does have a rejection handler. [EXPLAIN]

That's the mechanism. And notice the symmetry with Node 23, because it's the thing to hold onto:

**An exception walks down the stack looking for a catch. A rejection walks down the promise chain looking for a rejection handler.**

Same search, different data structure. The stack lives in the CPU's stack region and is destroyed when calls return; the chain is a set of blocks on the heap, connected by addresses, that survives exactly as long as anything references them (Node 22). That's why one works across time and the other can't.

So:

getUser(id)
  .then(u => getOrders(u.id))
  .then(o => getDetails(o[0].id))
  .then(d => render(d))
  .catch(e => showError(e));

One handler at the end catches a failure from any step. If getOrders rejects, its promise rejects, that rejection is adopted by the chain's next promise (Node 25's rule three, in reverse), and passes through every record with no rejection handler until it reaches the .catch.

And .catch is not a feature. **.catch(f) is literally .then(undefined, f)** — the same method with the fulfilment handler left out. .finally(f) is similarly sugar: run f regardless, and pass the original settlement through untouched, so it doesn't absorb a rejection or change a value.

Throwing works again, in the one place it can

Inside a handler, a throw becomes a rejection of p2 (Node 25, rule two). So this reads exactly like synchronous code and behaves correctly:

.then(res => {
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error("bad status " + res.status);
  return res.json();
})
.catch(e => showError(e));

That's the point at which promises stopped being "callbacks with better punctuation" and became a genuine control-flow mechanism: failure has one path, and one place to handle it, and it's the same path whether the failure came from the network or from your own code.

Three traps that are all mechanical once you see the chain

**.then(f, g) is not .then(f).catch(g).** In the two-argument form, f and g are the two handlers of one record, and only one of them ever runs. So if f itself throws, g is not consulted — g was for the previous promise's rejection, and that promise fulfilled. The rejection goes to whatever is after this record. In the chained form, catch is a later record, so it does see errors thrown by f. [USE] This is a real source of errors that vanish.

**A .then after a .catch still runs.** catch handles the rejection and returns a promise that fulfils (with whatever the handler returned) — because handling an error means the problem is dealt with. So the chain continues in the success direction. If you want it to stop, re-throw.

A rejection with nothing attached goes nowhere quietly. With callbacks, an ignored error at least reached the console. A rejected promise with no rejection handler anywhere just sits on the heap holding its reason. Browsers added a detector — after the microtask queue drains (Node 27), any promise that settled rejected with no handler fires an unhandledrejection event and logs a warning. It's a heuristic, not a guarantee, because you're allowed to attach a handler later, and the browser has to pick a moment to give up waiting. [USE]

The cost paid for all this

Stack traces get worse, and it isn't fixable in the naïve way. A stack trace (Node 5) is the pile of frames that exist right now. When your handler runs, that pile is two frames deep. The code that started the chain is nowhere in it — its frames were abandoned before the network even answered. So the trace tells you where the error surfaced and nothing about how you got there.

Engines eventually fixed this by cheating: V8 and the DevTools stitch together async stack traces, recording the stack at the moment a reaction was scheduled and splicing it on when the error is reported. That's why you see "async" separators in modern traces. It's reconstruction, not a real stack. [AWARE]

What you can do at this point: write a sequence of asynchronous steps with one failure path and one handler, and predict exactly where any given error lands.

What's still broken: Node 24 said reactions are "scheduled," and Node 19 only ever built one queue. If reactions go on that queue, then between two links of a chain the browser is free to run a click handler and repaint the screen — which turns out to be both a correctness problem and a speed problem.

sections.title: Node 27 — the second queue, and why it had to exist
sections.content:
The limitation: where, exactly, does a scheduled reaction go?

Try the obvious answer: onto Node 19's queue, as an ordinary entry — a task. Three things break.

Latency. The loop takes one entry per turn, and between turns it may do a render pass and dispatch pending input. A four-link chain would then take four turns of the loop. If a render happens each time, that's four screen refreshes at 16.67 ms each (Node 9), so a chain that does no real work at all takes ~67 ms to walk. Chains are common and often trivial — parse this JSON, pull out a field, hand it on. Paying a frame per link is absurd.

Visible inconsistency. Say the first link clears a list and the second fills it. If the browser can render between them, it can paint the empty list. The user sees a flash of nothing. From the code's point of view these are two lines of one operation; from the loop's point of view they're two separately scheduled entries with a render opportunity in the gap.

Ordering with everything else. Tasks come from many sources — clicks, timers, network completions. If reactions are tasks, then a promise that's already settled schedules a reaction that lands behind a click that arrived a millisecond ago. Your "immediately after this" is now after arbitrary unrelated work, and the ordering depends on real-world timing. Nothing is reliably reasonable about.

So a second queue was added, with a different rule.

The microtask queue

After the current task's function returns, and before the loop does anything else — before rendering, before the next task — drain the microtask queue completely. And "completely" means: keep going until it is empty, including microtasks added by microtasks.

The loop from Node 19, correctly:

forever:
    take the oldest TASK from the task queue
    call its function, wait for it to return
    ── drain the MICROTASK queue until empty ──   ← this is new
    if it's time for a frame: style, layout, paint

The specification calls that drain a microtask checkpoint. Promise reactions go on the microtask queue. So does queueMicrotask(fn), which is the plain "put this in that queue" primitive, and MutationObserver's callback — which is historically interesting, because before queueMicrotask existed, libraries got at this queue by creating a dummy DOM node and mutating it, purely as a way to hitch a ride. [AWARE]

All three problems dissolve. A whole chain runs in one checkpoint, within one turn of the loop, with no render in between — so it's fast, and no intermediate state is ever painted, and reactions always run before any pending task regardless of what arrived when.

The ordering, once, so you can derive it forever

console.log("1");
setTimeout(()   => console.log("2"), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("3"));
console.log("4");

Prints 1, 4, 3, 2.

Not a rule to memorise — read it off the loop. 1 and 4 are the current task running to completion (Node 19). setTimeout writes an entry in the timer table which becomes a task (Node 20). .then on a settled promise schedules a microtask. The current task returns; the checkpoint drains microtasks, so 3. Only then does the loop come round for the next task, so 2.

setTimeout(fn, 0) and queueMicrotask(fn) look like the same idea and are in different queues, and this is the entire difference.

The hazard the design creates

The drain runs until empty. So a microtask that queues another microtask, forever, is never interrupted:

function spin() { Promise.resolve().then(spin); }
spin();   // the page is gone. Permanently.

The loop never reaches the render step, never reaches the next task, and there is no timer interrupt for this (Node 6 — JavaScript is cooperative, on purpose, Node 19). The tab is unrecoverable and must be killed.

Compare setTimeout(spin, 0), which recurses through tasks — greedy and battery-hungry, but the loop still reaches the render step and still dispatches clicks between turns, so the page stays usable. The two queues have genuinely different failure modes, and that's the practical reason to know which one you're putting work on. [EXPLAIN]

There's a milder version of the same thing: a long chain of promise reactions that each do real work runs entirely inside one checkpoint, with no rendering in between. Promises are not a way to avoid blocking the page — they are a way to avoid blocking while waiting. Work is work, and work on the main thread costs frames whichever queue delivered it. That distinction is the one people most often get wrong when they say "make it async so it doesn't block." [EXPLAIN]

One aside, since it's in your stack

Node.js has this loop too, with the same microtask queue — and one extra: process.nextTick, which is drained before promise microtasks, for historical reasons predating promises. It's a Node-only wrinkle, and it's the kind of detail that shows up in interviews about the event loop. [AWARE]

What you can do at this point: predict the exact order of any mixture of synchronous code, promise reactions, and timers, by reading it off the loop rather than recalling a rule.

What's still broken: everything so far handles one pending thing at a time, in sequence. Node 23's third cost — coordinating several at once — was promised a fix once pending results became values. Node 28 collects.

Next: Node 28 — waiting for several things at once, and then Node 29 returns to Node 5's law that a function cannot pause, which is the last thing standing between us and await.

sections.title: Node 28 — waiting for several things at once
sections.content:
The limitation: Node 23's third cost — coordinating several pending things — was left open on the promise that it becomes writable once when pending results are values. Time to collect.

Here is Promise.all, in full, in terms of Node 24's boxes:

function all(promises) {
  return new Promise(function (resolve, reject) {
    const results = [];
    let remaining = promises.length;
    if (remaining === 0) return resolve(results);
    promises.forEach(function (p, i) {
      Promise.resolve(p).then(
        function (value) {
          results[i] = value;                 // by index, not arrival order
          remaining = remaining - 1;
          if (remaining === 0) resolve(results);
        },
        reject                                 // any rejection rejects the whole thing
      );
    });
  });
}

That's the same counter-and-array pattern from Node 23's hand-rolled version. Two things are different, and they're the whole point.

It's written once. By someone who thought about the error case, tested, and standardised — so nobody re-implements it slightly wrong in every codebase.

It handles the error case correctly, in one word: passing reject as the rejection handler for every element. Node 23's hand-rolled version hung forever on an error because its counter never reached zero. Here, any rejection rejects the outer promise immediately — and since a promise settles exactly once (Node 24), later rejections from the other elements are silently ignored rather than causing chaos.

And this was only writable because a pending result became a value. You cannot put callbacks in an array. [EXPLAIN]

The four collectors

**Promise.all(list) — fulfils with an array of every value, in the order of the input list**, not the order they finished. Rejects as soon as any one rejects. ES2015.

**Promise.race(list) — settles with the first to settle**, whether that's a fulfilment or a rejection. Its main real use is a timeout:

Promise.race([ fetchThing(), rejectAfter(5000) ])

ES2015.

**Promise.allSettled(list)** — never rejects. Waits for every one, and fulfils with an array of {status: "fulfilled", value} or {status: "rejected", reason}. This is what you want for "load six widgets, show whichever worked." Added in ES2020, five years later, because everyone kept hand-writing it by mapping each promise through a .catch that converts a rejection into a value.

**Promise.any(list) — fulfils with the first fulfilment**, ignoring rejections; if every one rejects, it rejects with an AggregateError holding all the reasons. "Try these three mirrors, take whichever answers." ES2021.

The misconception this is the right place to kill

**Promise.all does not make anything run in parallel.**

Look at the code again: it never starts anything. It receives promises that already exist. And a promise exists because somebody already called the thing that does the work — fetch(url) fires the request during the call (Node 21: hand it to the network machinery and return immediately).

So the concurrency was decided at the moment the array was built, not at all:

// three requests already in flight before this line finishes
const ps = urls.map(u => fetch(u));
await Promise.all(ps);      // just waits

versus

for (const u of urls) {
  await fetch(u);           // starts one, waits, starts the next
}

The second is sequential — three round trips end to end, Node 8's cost paid three times — not because await is slow but because the second request is not created until the first resolves. Promise.all is a collector, not a starter. [EXPLAIN]

This is the practical face of a deeper property: promises are eager. The work begins when the promise is created. (Some languages made the other choice — a "future" that doesn't start until awaited — and each has its own trap. JavaScript is eager, permanently, and every "why did it fetch even though I never awaited it" question comes from that.)

And what these still can't do

They can't cancel. Promise.race with a timeout resolves your chain early and the slow request keeps running, keeps holding memory, and still completes into nothing. Node 24's box has no stop button, because it doesn't know what work made it. Cancellation had to be added outside the promise system entirely — AbortController, Node 32.

They can't limit concurrency. Promise.all over a thousand URLs starts a thousand requests at once, and the browser's own connection limit (about six per host, from HTTP/1.1) turns that into a long queue with a thousand pending objects. There is no built-in "at most five at a time," which is why every codebase eventually grows a small limiter or pulls in one. [USE]

What you can do at this point: coordinate any number of pending operations, in any combination, with correct error behaviour, using code you didn't write.

What's still broken: the code still doesn't look like what it does. A chain of .then calls is a flat list of handlers, not a sequence of statements — there are no ordinary local variables spanning steps, no if around a step, no for loop that awaits each iteration, no try/catch. Every one of those has a promise-shaped workaround, and all of them are clumsy. What you want is to write it as ordinary code and have it pause. Node 5 says that's impossible.

sections.title: Node 29 — why a function, as built in Node 5, cannot pause
sections.content:
The limitation: everything we actually want reduces to one sentence — stop in the middle of a function, let the event loop run for 200 milliseconds, then continue from exactly where we stopped with every local variable intact.

Take Node 5 seriously for a moment, because it makes this look flatly impossible.

A running function's identity is its stack frame: a block of boxes holding its locals and its return address, sitting in the stack region, located by the stack pointer register. The frames form a pile, released strictly in reverse order.

Now try to pause. The function stops mid-body and control has to go back to the event loop (Node 19) so the browser can do things. Going back to the loop means the loop's frame is executing again, which means the stack pointer must move back past your frame — and Node 5 was explicit: those boxes are now available, and the very next function call will write over them. Your locals are gone. Not hidden. Overwritten by whatever ran next.

So you cannot have both. Either your frame stays on the stack — in which case everything below it is stuck, the stack pointer can't move past, and that's exactly blocking (Node 21's synchronous XHR, and the frozen tab) — or control returns to the loop and your frame is destroyed.

One contiguous stack region and one moving pointer cannot express "pause here." [EXPLAIN] That's not a JavaScript limitation. It's what a stack is.

The three ways out, and why one was chosen

Way one: give the function its own stack. If pausing is impossible on a shared stack, give each pausable thing a private stack region and swap the stack pointer between them — Node 7's context switch, done voluntarily rather than by a timer. This is real and widely used: coroutines in Lua, fibers, goroutines in Go.

It wasn't taken for JavaScript in the browser, for a specific and physical reason. The JavaScript stack is not a clean stack of JavaScript frames. It's interleaved with the browser's own C++ frames — your handler was called by the event loop's C++, which was called by the browser's C++, and a callback into JavaScript from a DOM method sits between more C++ frames. Swapping stacks under that would mean capturing and restoring engine and browser state that isn't designed to be moved, in every engine, forever. It also multiplies memory: each stack needs a region reserved (Node 5's megabytes), and pages create thousands of pending operations.

Way two: turn "the rest of the function" into a function. If the code after the pause point can't stay on the stack, move it to the heap where things survive (Node 22) — by making it a closure, and handing that closure to whoever will finish first.

This has a name, continuation-passing style, and you have been doing it by hand for six nodes. That's exactly what a callback is: the rest of my function, extracted into a closure, handed over. Node 23's costs are the cost of doing this transformation by hand, in your source, where a human has to read it.

Way three: have the compiler do way two, mechanically. Keep writing ordinary sequential code. Let the engine rewrite the function into a form that never needs to pause, because it was chopped into pieces at the pause points, with its variables moved somewhere that survives between them.

Way three is what happened, and it's the answer to a question worth asking out loud: **await does not add a new capability to the machine.** Nothing in Node 0 through Node 5 changed. What was added is a transformation, applied by the engine, that produces exactly the callback code you would have written yourself — while letting you write the readable version.

The name for a function that can pause and resume is a coroutine, and the mechanism way three uses is a state machine. Node 30 builds it. [EXPLAIN]

What you can do at this point: say precisely why pausing is impossible on the stack, and why that means the only options are a second stack or a rewrite.

What's still broken: "the compiler rewrites it" is hand-waving until you've seen the rewrite.

sections.title: Node 30 — generators: a function turned inside out
sections.content:
The limitation: we need to see the transformation, or way three is magic.

JavaScript got the mechanism in ES2015, as a feature that looks unrelated to async and is the whole engine of it. It came in from other languages first: Python had generators in 2001, C# had yield return in 2005, and Firefox shipped a non-standard version in 2006.

function* counter() {
  console.log("start");
  const a = yield 1;
  console.log("got", a);
  const b = yield 2;
  console.log("got", b);
  return "done";
}

const g = counter();        // nothing has run yet
g.next();                   // logs "start", returns { value: 1, done: false }
g.next("A");                // logs "got A",   returns { value: 2, done: false }
g.next("B");                // logs "got B",   returns { value: "done", done: true }

Read what that does, because it's exactly Node 29's impossible thing. The function runs to yield 1 and stops mid-body. Control returns to the caller — the stack unwinds completely, the event loop could run for an hour — and then g.next("A") continues from that line, with a bound to "A", and console.log still knowing everything it knew.

And it isn't magic. Here's the rewrite.

What the engine actually produces

The engine looks at the function and sees two things: its locals (a, b) and its pause points (two yields, splitting the body into three segments). It then produces, roughly, this:

function counter() {
  // The frame, moved to the heap (Node 22). Survives returns.
  const state = { step: 0, a: undefined, b: undefined };

  return {
    next: function (sent) {
      switch (state.step) {
        case 0:
          console.log("start");
          state.step = 1;
          return { value: 1, done: false };     // ← pause: just a return

        case 1:
          state.a = sent;                        // ← the value passed into next()
          console.log("got", state.a);
          state.step = 2;
          return { value: 2, done: false };

        case 2:
          state.b = sent;
          console.log("got", state.b);
          state.step = 3;
          return { value: "done", done: true };
      }
    }
  };
}

Three things happened, and none of them break any law from Part I:

The locals left the stack. a and b live in a heap block (Node 22), reachable from the generator object, so garbage collection keeps them alive as long as you hold g. This is the same trick as a closure — code plus a heap block of captured state — applied to a whole function body.

The body was chopped at the pause points into segments, and a switch on a number picks which one to run. Node 3: a switch is a compare and a conditional jump. Nothing exotic.

"Pausing" is just returning, and "resuming" is just calling again. The stack unwinds completely at each yield, exactly as Node 5 requires. Nothing is suspended in the CPU's sense. The illusion of a paused function is produced entirely by where the variables live plus a number saying which segment is next. [EXPLAIN]

Two directions of communication, both of which matter:

  • Out: yield 1 returns a value to whoever called next.
  • In: g.next("A") passes a value into the generator, which becomes the result of the yield expression that paused it.

That two-way channel is the piece that makes the next node possible. A generator can say "I need this," stop, and be handed the answer.

The obvious idea, which somebody had in 2013

Look at the shape:

  • A generator can yield a request and stop.
  • A promise (Node 24) is a request as a value that will settle later.

So: write a generator that yields promises, and write a small loop — a driver — that takes each yielded promise, attaches a reaction (Node 25), and when it settles, calls next(theValue) to resume the generator with the answer.

function drive(genFn) {
  const g = genFn();
  return new Promise(function (resolve, reject) {
    (function step(sent, thrown) {
      let r;
      try {
        r = thrown ? g.throw(thrown) : g.next(sent);   // resume the generator
      } catch (e) {
        return reject(e);                              // it threw: fail the outer promise
      }
      if (r.done) return resolve(r.value);             // it finished
      Promise.resolve(r.value).then(                   // it yielded a promise: wait
        v => step(v, null),                            // then resume with the value
        e => step(null, e)                             // or resume by throwing into it
      );
    })();
  });
}

Twenty lines. And now:

drive(function* () {
  const user    = yield getUser(id);
  const orders  = yield getOrders(user.id);
  const details = yield getDetails(orders[0].id);
  render(details);
});

Ordinary sequential code. Real local variables that span steps. You could wrap it in try/catch and it would work, because g.throw(e) injects the error at the paused line inside the generator, where a real try block really is on the real stack at that moment.

This existed as a library — **co, by TJ Holowaychuk, in 2013 — and it was widely used. Which is the thing to take from this node: async/await was invented, in userland, out of two features that already existed, two years before the language got it.** No new capability was required. It was a generator, a promise, and a twenty-line loop.

What you can do at this point: explain what a paused function physically is — a heap block of variables plus a number saying which segment runs next — and see that promises plus generators already contain everything await does.

What's still broken: you have to write function*, yield, and drag in a driver. The language should just do this. Node 31 is the language doing it, plus the one sentence about await that fixes most of the confusion around it.

Next: **Node 31 — async and await**, where the driver from this node moves into the engine, await turns out not to wait, and the "colour" of functions gets a mechanical explanation rather than a complaint.

sections.title: Node 31 — async and await
sections.content:
The limitation: Node 30 got there — real sequential code, real locals, real try/catch — but you had to write function*, remember yield, and import somebody's driver. The language should do this itself.

It does, and the mapping is exact.

The feature came from C#, where Anders Hejlsberg's team shipped async/await in C# 5.0 in 2012 (itself descended from F# async workflows in 2007). A JavaScript proposal followed in 2014, and it landed in ECMAScript 2017, shipping in Chrome in December 2016, Node 7.6 in February 2017, and Firefox in March 2017. People had been using it earlier through Babel, which compiled it down to exactly the generator-and-driver of Node 30.

Two rules. That's the entire feature.

**1. An async function always returns a promise, and it returns it immediately.**

>

**2. await X means: yield X to the built-in driver.**

The driver is the twenty lines from Node 30, moved inside the engine. The state machine is the rewrite from Node 30, done by the compiler. Nothing else was added to the machine — and I want that to be concrete, so here is the same code twice:

async function load(id) {
  const user    = await getUser(id);
  const orders  = await getOrders(user.id);
  return orders;
}
function load(id) {                      // what the engine effectively builds
  return drive(function* () {
    const user   = yield getUser(id);
    const orders = yield getOrders(user.id);
    return orders;
  });
}

Same thing. async is drive(function* (){...}) and await is yield.

The sentence that fixes most of the confusion

**await does not wait.**

Nothing waits. Nothing can wait — Node 21 and Node 29 established that with one thread there is no such operation. What await does is return.

Precisely, at an await:

  1. The engine hands the awaited value to the driver, which attaches a reaction to it (Node 25) — the reaction being "resume this state machine with the value."
  2. The function's live locals are already on the heap (Node 30), and the resume point — a number — is written into that heap block.
  3. The function returns. Its stack frame is popped, exactly as Node 5 requires. The stack unwinds all the way back to the event loop.
  4. The event loop carries on: next task, clicks dispatched, style, layout, paint. Node 19, undisturbed.
  5. Some time later the awaited promise settles. Its reaction goes on the microtask queue (Node 27). At the next checkpoint, the driver calls into the state machine, which jumps to the saved resume point, reads its locals out of the heap block, and carries on as if nothing happened.

The function was not paused. It was dismantled and stored, and later rebuilt. [EXPLAIN] "Pausing" is an illusion produced by keeping the variables somewhere the stack can't destroy and remembering a number.

Once you hold that, a whole family of behaviours stops needing rules:

**The part before the first await runs synchronously.** Calling an async function is an ordinary call: a frame goes on, the body runs, and it runs until it hits an await — only then does it return the promise. So:

async function go() { console.log("A"); await null; console.log("C"); }
go(); console.log("B");      // A, B, C

A is inside the function, before any await, in the same task. Then the function returns at the await, B runs, the task ends, the microtask checkpoint runs the resumption, C.

**await on a non-promise still costs a tick.** await null has nothing to wait for, and still returns and resumes on a microtask, because the driver goes through Promise.resolve regardless. So await always yields control at least once.

**The ordering rules of await are the ordering rules of .then**, because it is .then. If you can read the loop (Node 27), you never need to memorise await ordering.

*(A small performance footnote for completeness: the original specification made a single await allocate extra intermediate promises and cost three microtask ticks. V8 changed this in 2018 — the spec was amended alongside — bringing it to one. So the old advice that await is meaningfully slower than .then is obsolete.)*

Why try/catch works again

Node 23 was categorical: an exception can only walk the stack that currently exists, and a callback's stack is two frames deep, so the try you wrote is gone.

But look at what a resumed async function actually is. The driver calls into the state machine, so a real frame goes on the stack, running a segment of your function body. And that segment contains your try block — because the compiler kept the try in the segments it wraps. So the handler genuinely exists on the real stack at the moment the error is raised.

And the error is raised at the right place: when the awaited promise rejects, the driver resumes the machine with g.throw(reason) (Node 30), which injects the throw at the paused line. So:

async function load(id) {
  try {
    const user = await getUser(id);      // rejects
    return await getOrders(user.id);
  } catch (e) {
    return fallback();                   // genuinely catches it
  }
}

works for a mechanical reason, not a special-cased one. [EXPLAIN] This is arguably the single largest practical win of the whole feature: after Node 23's error-first callbacks and Node 26's chain-walking, failure handling is back to the thing you already knew.

The "colour" problem, explained rather than complained about

Here's the part that has been exhausting you, and it deserves a mechanical answer instead of a shrug.

async function getName() { return await fetchName(); }

const name = getName();     // a Promise, not a string. Always.

You cannot get the value out into ordinary synchronous code. You can only await it — which requires you to be async — which infects your caller, and theirs, all the way up. Bob Nystrom named this in a 2015 essay, "What Color Is Your Function?": the language has two kinds of function and they don't mix, and once one thing in your program is asynchronous, everything above it is too.

The reason is Node 29, exactly and completely. To hand the value back to a synchronous caller, that caller would have to pause at the call site while the loop ran. Its frame would have to survive the stack unwinding. It can't — it wasn't compiled into a state machine, its locals are in a stack frame, and there is nothing to resume. **Only a function the compiler rewrote can be resumed, and the compiler only rewrites the ones you marked async.** The colour isn't a taste decision or an oversight. It's which functions got the transformation.

And the transformation isn't free, which is why it isn't just applied to everything: locals move to the heap (Node 22), the body is split into segments, and every call allocates a promise and a state block.

So the honest summary of Part IV so far: the single thread bought you freedom from locks and races, and the bill is that "asynchronous" is a property that propagates up your entire call graph. That's the trade, all the way back to Node 18, and it is not going away.

Two mistakes that are now obvious

**await in a loop is sequential.** Node 28 said Promise.all doesn't start anything; the concurrency is decided when the promises are created. So:

for (const u of urls) { results.push(await fetch(u)); }   // one at a time
const results = await Promise.all(urls.map(u => fetch(u))); // all at once

In the first, the second fetch isn't created until the first resolves — three round trips end to end (Node 8). In the second, all the fetches are created in one synchronous pass, so all are in flight, and Promise.all merely waits. [USE]

**await does not make anything faster or unblock anything.** It yields while waiting. Work is still work: an async function doing a 500 ms computation between two awaits blocks the loop for 500 ms exactly like a normal function (Node 19). Async is about not blocking during Node 8's nineteen years, not about doing work off the main thread — which needs Node 35.

One late addition: await at the top level of a file was originally illegal, because a script's top level is not a function and there's nothing to rewrite. ES2022 allowed it in modules, where the module system can treat the whole module as an async unit and make importers wait. Still illegal in classic scripts, for the mechanical reason. [AWARE]

What you can do at this point: write asynchronous code as ordinary sequential code, and explain every one of its behaviours by pointing at a heap block, a resume number, and a microtask queue.

What's still broken: the API this is all pointed at is still XMLHttpRequest from 1999 — an event-based, stateful object with a readyState counter, built before promises existed, and defined loosely enough that browsers disagreed on details for a decade.

sections.title: Node 32 — fetch, and a response that arrives in pieces
sections.content:
The limitation: XHR's shape predates everything in Part IV, and its specification predates any precise model of what a browser does when it makes a request.

The second half of that sentence matters more than the first. By around 2011 the browser's networking behaviour — how redirects are followed, when a cache entry is usable, what a cross-origin request is allowed to do (Nodes 33 and 34) — was implemented four times, differently, and specified nowhere coherently. The Fetch Standard, edited by Anne van Kesteren at the WHATWG, was written to define that whole model once: what a request is, what a response is, and exactly what the browser does in between. fetch() is the JavaScript-facing door onto that model, and it's why images, stylesheets, XHR and fetch are now all described as the same machinery with different entry points. [AWARE]

It shipped in Chrome in April 2015 and Firefox in July 2015.

const res  = await fetch("/messages");
const data = await res.json();

Why there are two awaits

This is the design's most instructive detail, and people read it as clumsiness.

**The first promise resolves when the response headers have arrived — not the body.**

Recall Node 10: a response arrives as packets, ~1500 bytes at a time, over Node 8's slow link. A large response arrives over many round trips. XHR made you wait for all of it (its readyState 4), which means for a 10-megabyte download you had one moment of "nothing" followed by one moment of "everything."

fetch splits that. Headers arrive first — status code, content type, whether it's a redirect — so you can decide what to do before a single byte of body exists. Then res.json() or res.text() reads the body, which takes as long as it takes, and returns a second promise. [EXPLAIN]

And underneath, res.body is a stream: an object you can pull chunks from as they arrive. Streams have two properties worth naming, because they're the general answer to "data bigger than memory":

  • You process it in pieces, so a 2-gigabyte download never needs 2 gigabytes of heap.
  • Backpressure: the consumer pulls, so if you're reading slowly, the browser stops asking the network for more, and TCP's flow control (Node 10) propagates that all the way back to the server. Without it, a fast producer and a slow consumer means an unbounded buffer, which means memory exhaustion.

That's how you show a download progress bar, and how a streamed LLM response gets rendered token by token instead of appearing all at once.

Because the body is a stream, it can be read exactly once — the bytes are consumed. Read it twice and you get an error. res.clone() exists for when you genuinely need two readers, and it costs buffering. [USE]

The gotcha everyone hits once

**fetch does not reject on 404 or 500.** It fulfils.

It rejects only when the HTTP exchange didn't happen — DNS failure, connection refused, the network dropped, a CORS rule blocked it (Node 34).

This looks wrong and is defensible: a 404 is a successful conversation in which the server clearly answered "not found." The request worked. The transport worked. The answer is a legitimate answer, and throwing it away as an exception would discard the response object that contains it.

But it means this is broken:

try {
  const res = await fetch(url);
  const data = await res.json();   // silently parses the 500 page's HTML → throws a confusing syntax error
} catch (e) { ... }

and the fix is mandatory in every codebase:

const res = await fetch(url);
if (!res.ok) throw new Error("HTTP " + res.status);

res.ok is true for statuses 200–299. [USE] Every wrapper library you've seen around fetch exists mostly to do that check and to add a base URL.

Cancellation, added from outside

Node 28 left a hole: promises cannot be cancelled, because a promise is a box that doesn't know what work filled it (Node 24).

The fix couldn't be in the promise, so it was built as a separate object pair — an **AbortController** with a signal you hand to fetch:

const controller = new AbortController();
const p = fetch(url, { signal: controller.signal });
controller.abort();          // p rejects with an AbortError

Note what's happening: abort() doesn't cancel the promise, it tells the network machinery to stop, and that machinery then rejects the promise. The signal is a channel to the work, running alongside the promise that reports the result. It shipped around 2017–2018, and it's now the standard way anything cancellable in the platform is cancelled — the same controller works for addEventListener, for streams, and for your own code, which can check signal.aborted or listen for its abort event. [USE]

This is a good example of a pattern worth recognising in the platform: when a primitive is missing a capability, the web usually grows a second object beside it rather than changing the first, because the first can't change without breaking everything already written.

The options that turn into Part V

fetch(url, options) takes a handful of settings that look like plumbing and are actually the entire security model:

  • **mode** — cors, no-cors, same-origin: what kind of cross-site request this is allowed to be.
  • **credentials** — omit, same-origin, include: whether the user's cookies go with it.
  • **headers** — some of which you are forbidden to set, because the browser guarantees their truth.

Every one of those exists because of the sentence at the end of Node 21: a page can now silently make requests to any machine, in the background, with whatever credentials the browser holds. Part V is what had to be built to make that survivable.

What you can do at this point: make any HTTP request from a page, handle its response as it arrives, cancel it, and say exactly which failures are exceptions and which are answers.

What's still broken: nothing has yet stopped a page from fetching your bank's account page, with your logged-in cookies attached, and posting the result to a server in another country.

Part IV is complete. The whole arc, in one line: one thread meant the pleasant API was impossible → callbacks were the only tool and cost four specific things → making the pending result a value fixed all four → chaining needed then to return a new promise → errors travel that chain instead of the stack → reactions needed their own queue → a function can't pause, so the compiler rewrites it into a state machine with heap-allocated locals → await is yield to a built-in driver, and it doesn't wait, it returns.

Next: Part V, starting with Node 33 — the origin, which is the answer to the question Node 21 opened and never closed.

sections.title: PART V — THE PLATFORM
Node 33 — the origin
sections.content:
The limitation: Node 21 ended with a sentence that was left hanging: a page can now run code and silently make requests to any machine, with whatever credentials the browser holds. Nothing has said what a page is allowed to reach.

Think about what a browser actually is at this point, in terms of Part I. It's a process (Node 6) with several threads (Node 7), holding in its memory the document trees, variables, cookies and open connections of every site you have open at once. Your bank in one tab. A stranger's page in another. Both running code the sites wrote, in the same browser, on the same machine, with access to the same interpreter and the same network stack.

If nothing separates them, then a page from anywhere can read the DOM of your bank tab, or fetch your account page and post the result somewhere. Which would make the web unusable for anything that matters — and this was recognised immediately, in 1995, when Netscape shipped JavaScript. The same-origin policy arrived in Navigator 2.0, alongside the language, because a language that can fetch and read is only safe if something bounds it.

What an origin is

Everything is keyed to a triple:

origin = (scheme, host, port)

https://example.com:443. All three must match, exactly, for two pages to be the same origin. [EXPLAIN]

  • Host must match because that's the whole point — evil.com isn't bank.com. And it's a string match: bank.com and app.bank.com are different origins, and no relationship is inferred from the shared suffix.
  • Scheme must match because http:// has no integrity guarantee — anyone on the network path can alter it (Node 10 — packets pass through routers). If http://bank.com counted as the same origin as https://bank.com, an attacker who could tamper with the plain page would inherit the secure one's data. So they're separate origins.
  • Port must match because two different programs can be listening on two ports of the same machine (Node 10), and they may be run by different people — a shared university host, a development machine.

The rule, and the thing everybody gets backwards

The same-origin policy says, roughly: code running in origin A may not read data belonging to origin B. That covers reading another window's DOM, reading a response from another origin, and reading another origin's storage and cookies.

And now the part that is genuinely counter-intuitive, and that explains half of web security:

**The same-origin policy restricts reading responses. It does not restrict sending requests.**

Your page may freely cause requests to any origin: <img src="https://other.com/pic.png"> loads and displays. <script src="https://cdn.com/lib.js"> loads and runs, in your origin. A <form> may submit to any host. A stylesheet, an iframe, a video — all cross-origin, all fine.

Why on earth allow that? Because by 1995 the web was already made of it. Images hosted elsewhere, links to anywhere, forms posting to other services. A rule that blocked cross-origin requests would have broken the existing web on the day it shipped, and would have been ignored. So the policy was drawn where it could be drawn: you can cause the request, you just can't see the answer. [EXPLAIN]

Hold that line — "sending is free, reading is controlled" — because Node 34's two big topics are each one side of it. CSRF is an attack that needs only sending. CORS is a mechanism for permitting reading.

The browser is the enforcer, and that's the whole model

Nothing in the same-origin policy happens on a server. The server has no idea. It receives a request, and it answers.

The enforcement is entirely in the browser, which is choosing not to hand a received response to the JavaScript that asked for it. The bytes arrived. They're in the browser's memory. The interpreter is refusing to expose them (Node 18 — the interpreter decides what's allowed, because the script never becomes machine code).

Three consequences, and they resolve a lot of confusion:

**curl has no same-origin policy.** Nor does a server, a mobile app, or a script of yours. These rules protect a user sitting at a browser from pages they didn't choose to trust. They are not a server-side access control, and a server that relies on them for security has no security at all.

A CORS error is not the server rejecting you. The request was sent. The server ran it. If it was a POST that charged a card, the card was charged. The browser simply refused to let your JavaScript read the reply. This is why "I got a CORS error so my request didn't go through" is usually wrong. [EXPLAIN]

Origins are a security principal, and the whole platform is keyed to them. localStorage, IndexedDB, the cache, permissions you've granted for camera or location, service workers — every one of them is partitioned by origin. Two pages on the same origin share all of it; two pages one character apart in hostname share none of it.

And since 2018, Chrome backs this with Part I's real isolation: Site Isolation puts different sites in different processes (Node 6), so cross-site data isn't merely un-exposed by the interpreter, it's in a different memory world with no address that reaches it. That was driven by Node 36's story, and it's the strongest form of the boundary.

The sanctioned holes

**window.postMessage.** Sometimes two origins genuinely want to talk — a page and an embedded widget. So there's one narrow, explicit channel: send a copy of a value to another window, which receives it as an event. It's the only cross-origin channel, and it's deliberately copy-only, so no live objects and no shared memory cross the line. The security burden is on the receiver, which must check event.origin — and forgetting that check is a classic real vulnerability. [USE]

**document.domain**, a 1990s mechanism letting two pages on related subdomains agree to relax into a shared origin, has been deprecated and disabled, because it lets one compromised subdomain reach into others.

The hole that isn't sanctioned

The policy protects origin B's data from code in origin A. So think about what happens if an attacker gets code into origin B.

Then there's nothing to protect you with. Their code is B. It reads B's DOM, B's cookies, B's storage, and can fetch B's endpoints with B's credentials, and the same-origin policy defends it while it does. That's cross-site scripting (XSS), and it's the reason it is such a severe class of bug: it doesn't break the boundary, it puts the attacker inside it. [EXPLAIN]

Which is also why the platform later grew Content Security Policy (around 2012–2013): a header where a site says which origins its scripts may come from and whether inline <script> is allowed at all — so that even if an attacker injects a tag, the browser refuses to run it. A second fence inside the first.

What you can do at this point: say exactly what a page may reach and why, and where the boundary is enforced.

What's still broken: "sending requests is free" is fine as long as a request carries no authority. It doesn't. The browser attaches your identity to outgoing requests automatically, and it does that based on where the request is going — not on who asked for it.

sections.title: Node 34 — cookies, and the exact reason CORS exists
sections.content:
The limitation: HTTP is stateless (Node 12) — the server answers and forgets you. So how does it know, on your second request, that you're the person who logged in?

Cookies, and the property that ruins everything

The answer, invented by Lou Montulli at Netscape in 1994, is small: the server sends a header, Set-Cookie: session=abc123, and the browser stores that string and attaches it to every subsequent request to that host, automatically, forever, until it expires.

It works. It's the foundation of every logged-in session on the web. And it has one property that turned out to be a decade-long security problem:

**The browser attaches cookies based on where the request is going, not on who initiated it.**

That's called ambient authority — your identity travels with the request regardless of who caused it. And now combine it with Node 33's line that sending is free:

A page on evil.com contains this:

<form action="https://bank.com/transfer" method="POST">
  <input name="to" value="attacker">
  <input name="amount" value="10000">
</form>
<script>document.forms[0].submit();</script>

Node 33 says a form may submit to any origin. The browser attaches your bank.com cookies because the request is going to bank.com. The bank receives a well-formed, fully authenticated POST from a logged-in user and does exactly what it says. The attacker never reads the response — they don't need to; the damage is in the sending.

That's cross-site request forgery (CSRF), and notice that the same-origin policy does nothing about it, correctly and by design, because nothing was read. [EXPLAIN]

The defences, in the order they were invented:

CSRF tokens. The server puts a random value in the page and requires it back with any state-changing request. evil.com can't read your bank's page (that is blocked), so it can't know the value. Effective, and it requires every endpoint to remember.

**SameSite cookies.** A flag on the cookie telling the browser to attach it only when the request comes from the same site. Chrome made SameSite=Lax the default in 2020, which kills the cross-site POST above outright. This is the platform fixing the 1994 default two and a half decades later, and it broke a lot of legitimate cross-site flows on the way, which is why it took so long. [USE]

And now CORS, which is not what you think it is

Here's the framing that turns CORS from a wall into a mechanism.

Node 33: your JavaScript may not read a response from another origin. That's the default, and it's the safe one. But plenty of legitimate cases need exactly that — a public API, your own frontend on app.example.com talking to your own backend on api.example.com (different host, therefore different origin, therefore blocked).

So a way was needed for the server being asked to say "this origin may read my responses." That mechanism is CORS — Cross-Origin Resource Sharing — worked on from around 2005, a W3C Recommendation in January 2014, and now part of the Fetch Standard from Node 32.

CORS is a relaxation of the same-origin policy, not a restriction added by it. It exists to let you do more than the default. You experience it as a wall because the default was already a wall, and CORS is the door.

[EXPLAIN] That reframing alone resolves most of the frustration, because it makes clear where the fix lives: on the server being called, always. There is no browser-side setting, and any "fix" that involves disabling browser security is not a fix.

How it actually works

The simple case. Your page at https://app.example.com calls fetch("https://api.other.com/data").

  1. The browser sends the request, adding a header: Origin: https://app.example.com. It sends it — Node 33, sending is free.
  2. The server answers. If it wants to allow this, it includes Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com (or * for "anyone").
  3. The browser receives the response, looks for that header, and: if it's there and matches, hands the response to your JavaScript. If not, it discards it and rejects your promise with an opaque error.

Step 3 is why the error message never tells you the status code or the body — the browser deliberately gives your script nothing, because telling you "it was a 403" would itself be leaking cross-origin information. [USE]

And re-read step 1 and 2: the request was sent, the server acted on it. CORS protects you from other sites reading your data. It has never protected a server from anything.

The preflight case, which is the part people find arbitrary and isn't.

For requests that are "not simple" — a PUT or DELETE, a custom header like Authorization, a Content-Type: application/json — the browser first sends a separate OPTIONS request asking permission, and only sends the real one if the answer allows it:

OPTIONS /data
Origin: https://app.example.com
Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT
Access-Control-Request-Headers: content-type

→ Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com
  Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, PUT
  Access-Control-Allow-Headers: content-type
  Access-Control-Max-Age: 86400

Why the distinction? The rule is: a request that an old-fashioned HTML form could already have sent doesn't need permission, because servers have always been exposed to it. A form can POST cross-origin with Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded — that's Node 34's CSRF, and servers have had twenty-five years to defend against it.

But a cross-origin DELETE, or a POST with Content-Type: application/json, was never previously possible. So there exist servers written before CORS that assumed "if it's a JSON PUT, it must have come from our own frontend," and used that assumption as a security boundary. If browsers had started sending those cross-origin without asking, every one of those servers would have been silently exposed on the day the feature shipped.

So preflight is a backward-compatibility safety mechanism: never send a kind of request that didn't used to be possible, until the server confirms it understands the new world. Access-Control-Max-Age lets the browser cache that answer so it isn't an extra round trip (Node 8) on every call. [EXPLAIN]

Credentials. By default, cross-origin fetch sends no cookies. To include them you must ask on both sides: credentials: "include" in the fetch, and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true from the server. And when credentials are involved, Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * is forbidden — the server must name the exact origin. Obviously so: "any origin may make authenticated requests and read the answers" would re-create the problem the whole node is about. [USE]

The hack that CORS killed, which is worth knowing

Before CORS, people still needed cross-origin data, and they found a hole in Node 33's line: <script src> is not blocked, and a loaded script runs in your origin.

So: JSONP. Ask the server for a script, and have it wrap the data in a function call.

<script src="https://api.other.com/data?callback=handleIt"></script>
<!-- server returns:  handleIt({"name": "..."})  -->

It's a real script, so it isn't blocked, and it calls your function with the data. Clever, widely used, and completely unsafe: you are executing whatever that server sends, inside your origin, with full access to your DOM and cookies. One compromised API and the attacker owns your page. It only supported GET, and had no error handling. It disappeared once CORS was universal, and it explains why CORS felt like such a relief rather than an obstacle. [AWARE]

The practical summary

When you hit a CORS error: the fix is a response header on the server you are calling. If you don't control that server, your options are a proxy you do control (server-to-server calls have no browser and therefore no CORS), or the API's own supported cross-origin route. Disabling browser security to make it go away in development produces code that fails for every user. [USE]

What you can do at this point: explain the entire browser security model as one line — sending is free, reading is controlled, cookies are attached automatically — and derive CSRF, CORS, preflight and JSONP from it rather than memorising them.

What's still broken: Part IV solved waiting without blocking. It did nothing about work. A 500-millisecond computation still freezes the page (Node 19), and no amount of async changes that, because there is still exactly one thread running your code.

Next: Node 35 — real threads in your hands, where the browser finally gives you a second thread, and where the shape of the API is dictated entirely by Node 18's decision that only one thread may touch the DOM.
